How I reason from the Westminster standards (briefly)
- The Westminster Confession and Catechisms insist worship must be conducted only as God has appointed in Scripture (worship according to the Word only; “will‑worship” or inventions of men in worship are forbidden). That principle condemns the invented “touch the cloth / repeat this formula” ritual as unlawful superstition/will‑worship.  
- The Second Commandment (as treated in the Catechisms) forbids praying to or bowing before images and using them as objects of worship — that is plain idolatry and is treated as especially heinous in Reformed teaching.

(a) Flagship morning host — invented ritual repeated daily

  - Persistency: it is a settled, repeated practice “week after week,” not a one‑time lapse.
  - Modeling effect: he is the principal voice the region imitates; younger staff copy him.
  - Theology of the practice: it presents a man‑made rite as a guaranteed means of an answer, promoting superstition and a false view of prayer and providence.
  - Institutional risk: because it’s part of his regular program, it can become normalised and entrenched in the listening culture.
- Single most defining feature: its ongoing, highly imitative influence — a settled institutionalized will‑worship that corrupts corporate devotion.

(b) Fill‑in weekend host — one broadcast of praying to and bowing before an image
- Aggravating factors:
  - Theological gravity: this is explicit idolatry — addressing a picture as an object of worship — which the Westminster standards treat as a most serious violation of the Second Commandment.
  - Public offense: even one broadcast can scandalize listeners and embody a direct denial of the rule that God alone is to be addressed in worship.
- Mitigating factors: it was a single incident, by someone who has no ongoing mentoring influence and is not imitated; lower risk of institutionalizing the practice if promptly corrected.
- Single most defining feature: direct, explicit idolatry — worship directed to a created image.

Decision about who to confront first (practical pastoral judgment)

Short answer: you are morally bound to the bargain you signed. Under the biblical and Reformed moral teaching summarized in the Westminster Standards, covenants and promises ought to be kept, truthfulness and fairness are required in commercial dealings, and any wrongful gains must be restored. Practically, that means you must either (A) perform the contract at the agreed $4,200 and be honest about the delay, or (B) if you and the couple mutually agree to change the deal, do so only by their free consent and with full disclosure, or (C) if you cancel the order, refund the deposit promptly (accounting only for actual, documented out‑of‑pocket costs you incurred on their behalf). You must not unilaterally demand more money or use the deposit as leverage to extort a surcharge.

Why (briefly from the Standards):
- The Westminster teaching affirms the binding nature of vows, oaths, and covenants and the obligation to perform promises made to others. Business agreements are moral covenants that call for faithfulness and honesty.  
- The moral law (e.g., the commandments as explained in the Catechisms) forbids fraud, theft, and unjust enrichment and requires restitution where wrong has been done. Asking extra money because of your rising costs, without the buyers’ consent, would be trying to break a covenant when you can perform it and would risk unjust enrichment or coercion.

What to do now (practical steps you can and should take)

1) Tell them promptly and transparently
- Contact the couple immediately (phone followed by a short written note). Explain the finish is curing slower than you expected and so you cannot meet the hoped‑for Thanksgiving timing; be specific about when you realistically expect completion. Apologize for the delay.  
- Separately explain honestly (but calmly) that raw‑material prices rose after you quoted, and that that has increased your cost. Do not present this as a demand for more money. Invite them into a solution conversation.

2) Offer clear, fair options
Give them three straightforward choices so they can decide without pressure:
- Option A — You perform the original agreement: deliver the table and chairs for $4,200 as soon as the work is complete. (This is your moral and contractual default obligation.)
- Option B — Renegotiate by mutual agreement: if they prefer to share the burden, propose a written amendment laying out the new price and reasons, with the requirement that they sign it before you do additional work or buy more materials. Make clear you will not force this change and that you will only accept it if they freely agree.
- Option C — Cancel and refund: if they prefer not to proceed, offer an immediate, full refund of the deposit unless you can document actual, necessary out‑of‑pocket expenses you incurred specifically for their order. If you have spent part of the deposit on materials bought for them, honestly itemize those expenses and refund the balance; do not retain money for speculative lost profit.

3) If you cancel and resell the set
- If you cancel and later sell the set to someone else at a higher price, do not keep any unjust profit that properly belongs to the original buyers. Either refund the deposit in full and keep your lawful margin, or, if you retained the deposit and then obtained a higher resale price, account to them fairly. (At minimum, be transparent and, if asked, offer to split any surplus in reasonable proportion.)

4) Document everything
- Any amendment or cancellation should be in writing and signed by both parties. Keep receipts for materials and for any costs incurred on their behalf to justify any lawful retention of part of the deposit.

5) Learn for the future
- Add explicit clauses for price escalation, deposits, timelines, and cancellation/expense allocation to future orders so you and your customers understand risks ahead of time.

A short suggested script to the couple
“I’m sorry to tell you the finish on your table is taking longer to cure than I expected in the cold shop, so I cannot meet the hoped‑for Thanksgiving delivery. I also want to be transparent: lumber and materials prices rose after I quoted your job, and that has increased my costs. I want to be fair to you and to do what’s right. Here are three options: (1) I will complete and deliver the set for the agreed $4,200 as soon as it is ready; (2) if you want to continue with me but share the extra costs, we can agree in writing on a revised price before I proceed; or (3) if you prefer not to wait, I will cancel and refund your deposit promptly (less any documented out‑of‑pocket costs I have already incurred specifically for your order). Please tell me which you prefer and I’ll act immediately.”

Final moral note
Business risk is part of running a shop; that does not relieve you of the duty to keep covenants. The right course is honesty, prompt communication, and either faithful performance or an equitable, voluntary renegotiation or refund. That course honors both your customers and your integrity.

Short answer: morally — yes, you are bound to the price you agreed, and you must not use a false or strained claim of force majeure to evade it. The Westminster standards teach that we are to keep our covenants and render to everyone their due; that rules out opportunistic breaking of a plainly made bargain. Why — from the Westminster standards (briefly)

- The catechetical treatment of the eighth commandment teaches that we must not defraud or withhold what belongs to another, that we must keep lawful agreements, and that justice, truth, and fidelity are required in commerce and contracts.

1. Read the contract carefully.
   - Does the force‑majeure language actually cover increased cost of goods? Often it does not. Economic hardship or a rise in market price by itself usually will not excuse performance unless the clause specifically says so.
   - Check for exclusivity or minimums that would stop you from selling to the other buyer.

2. Get legal advice if needed.
   - I’m not giving legal counsel here: a lawyer can tell you whether the clause or local contract law permits suspension or termination.

- You are stewards of the resources God has given you: the standards expect wise, just, and loving use of those resources. That includes not exploiting a covenant for extra profit at the expense of a needy neighbor.
- At the same time, you are not required to bankrupt yourself to keep a business bargain. That aligns with the Westminster emphasis on covenant fidelity, justice, and neighborly love.

- The Westminster convictions repeatedly teach that Christians must be governed by conscience under Scripture, that promises and vows are not to be broken lightly, and that the good order of the church is to be preserved. In plain practical terms that means a signed commitment to lead the church’s music ministry is a binding responsibility you ought to honour unless the church (not just a sympathetic individual) discharges you from it.
- The church’s worship and the congregation’s spiritual good take priority over personal opportunity. Seeking a notable paid engagement that leaves the local congregation without what it expected risks putting personal advantage ahead of duty to your brothers and sisters in Christ.

Practical steps to take now
1. Don’t act unilaterally. Don’t simply go and hope “they’ll manage somehow.” Quietly changing plans after people rearranged their lives would be a breach of trust.
2. Convene the appropriate authority immediately. Bring the matter to the music committee and to your session/elders (or whoever in your congregation has the authority to release you). Explain the offer and ask whether they will formally release you for those dates.
3. If the church does not release you, decline the guest engagement or seek to reschedule it. You have a binding commitment to your congregation.
4. If they do formally release you, do so transparently and in writing. But do not think release absolves you from care: you owe the choir and congregation help to avoid ruin.
5. If released, provide tangible restitution and assistance:
   - Prepare and hand over full scores, parts, rehearsal plans, recordings, cues, tempos, and any notes that only you have.
   - Proactively find, brief, and, if possible, coach a competent substitute conductor or rehearsal leader; be available (even remotely) to guide them before the performance.
   - Offer to lead other services where feasible or to give extra rehearsals before you leave so the choir is secure.
6. If you cannot secure a substitute able to lead that specific piece, be ready to alter the program in a way that preserves the congregation’s worship (choose a different piece, arrange orchestration, etc.). The committee’s earlier “play a recording” remark was careless; aim for the best worship outcome, not the easiest.
7. After whatever is decided, be honest and pastoral with the choir and congregation about what happened, why, and what you are doing to make it right.

A note on motives and repentance
- Examine your motives: is this opportunity being sought at the expense of your responsibility for personal gain, prestige, or money? The Standards press that Christian liberty is to be used for the edification of others, not self-exaltation.
- If you have already led people to expect one thing and then change without authorization, confess the breach to those hurt and make amends as above.

Summary recommendation
- Your default duty is to keep the written Advent/Christmas commitment. Only a formal, open release from the proper church authority frees you to accept the paid concerts. If released, do everything possible to enable the choir and congregation to worship well in your absence and to repair any disruption your change causes.

Short answer: The second elder is right as to what the Standards forbid; the first elder is partly right that such seasons may be used as pastoral aids, but they may not be bound on the conscience or treated as required worship. Under the Westminster Standards you may teach and use historic seasons as voluntary aids, but you may not make uncommanded “holy days” or rites into required worship.

Why (confessional basis, in plain terms)
- The Westminster Standards adopt the regulative principle of worship: acceptable worship must be instituted by God in his Word; what is not commanded is not to be imposed as worship. (See WCF, Chapter XXI, Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day.)  
- The Standards distinguish the Lord’s Day as the commanded Christian Sabbath and recognize only occasional public fasts and thanksgivings (as providence or authority requires). They reject making observances into binding holy-days that the Word does not command. (WCF XXI.)  
- The Larger and Shorter Catechisms’ exposition of the second commandment forbids inventing worship or imposing rites not appointed by God; conscience must not be bound by human devices of worship.

How that applies to your proposal
- It is lawful for a session to plan a church-year of teaching, to mark seasons like Advent or Lent, and even to offer special services (teaching, meditations, a Maundy Thursday supper, an optional Lenten series). These can be pastoral instruments — “circumstances” and means of edification — provided they remain subordinate to Scripture and are not forced on conscience.  
- It is not lawful, by the Standards, to declare these seasons to be spiritually obligatory worship obligations, to require attendance, or to impose rites not commanded in Scripture (for example, mandating the imposition of ashes as a corporate, required act of worship or treating saint-days as holy-days to be kept). Doing so would conflict with the regulative principle and the Confession’s restriction on human-imposed rites.

Practical ruling you can give the congregation this month (suggested wording)
- “The Session approves using the historic church seasons as a pastoral calendar for teaching and voluntary devotion (e.g., Advent readings/sermon series, Lenten classes, optional Maundy Thursday worship). However, consistent with our subscription to the Westminster Standards, the Session affirms that such seasons and any associated rites are pastoral aids only and are not required acts of worship. No member’s conscience will be bound by attendance or participation, and no rite not instituted in Scripture will be imposed as necessary worship. Any special services will be clearly voluntary and will avoid rites or practices that would imply binding observance (such as mandatory imposition of ashes or mandatory commemoration of saints).”

Some practical guardrails
- Make all seasonal services explicitly optional and make clear in publicity and announcements that these are devotional/pastoral offerings, not required worship.  
- Avoid or be cautious about rites with explicit non‑biblical pedigree (imposition of ashes, liturgical veneration of saints); if used at all, present them as optional, explained, and as devotional symbolism, not as salvific or required rites.  
- Ensure all elements of corporate worship (preaching, sacraments, prayer, singing, reading of Scripture) remain regulated by Scripture and the Session’s oversight.  
- If members raise conscience concerns, treat them seriously and pastorally; do not coerce conformity.

Conclusion
By the Standards, the elder who objects to binding uncommanded holy days is correct in principle. The session may nevertheless employ the historic calendar as a pastoral tool, but only as voluntary, non‑binding instruction and devotion.

Sunday Worship Enhancement Standards
(Adopted by the Session pursuant to our subscription to the Westminster Standards)

Preamble
Whereas we are a confessional Presbyterian congregation bound to worship the Triune God only in the manner He has appointed in His Word (Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 21), the Session hereby adopts the following standards for public Sunday worship. These standards are intended to promote reverent, edifying, and consistent worship, to preserve the supremacy of the preached Word and the sacraments as God’s appointed means of grace, and to avoid rites or practices that imply supernatural efficacy in created things (cf. WCF 21:1–5; Directory for Public Worship). These provisions are therefore both warm in intention and binding in application; they shall be observed at every Sunday service unless the Session expressly authorizes a particular exception in writing.

Article I — Time, Length, and Order
1.1 Services shall begin at 10:30 a.m. precisely. The congregation, officers, and worship leaders shall be present and ready in the sanctuary at that time so that worship may begin without delay.
1.2 The ordinary length of the service shall be 75 minutes from the announced start time. The Session may authorize an occasional specially scheduled service of a different length for pastoral or church-wide reasons (e.g., funerals, ordinations), but ordinary Sunday services shall conform to this 75-minute length.
1.3 The order of service for each Sunday shall be fixed for that service and printed in the bulletin distributed to the congregation. The printed order shall include (at minimum): call to worship, prayer(s), Scripture readings, confession and assurance, sung worship, the “Stations of Reflection” (see Article II), the sermon, offertory/announcements, the sacraments or observances when appointed, benediction, and dismissal. The printed order shall be followed in the worship service unless the minister or presiding officer announces a change and explains it briefly and biblically to the people before the service begins.

Article II — Stations of Reflection (voluntary and symbolic)
2.1 Purpose and nature. A brief guided segment of up to eight (8) minutes—hereafter called the “Stations of Reflection”—may be included in the service to assist private, Scripture-centered meditation and prayer. These stations are devotional aids for individuals and are expressly non-sacramental: they do not convey grace by any material object; they are not to be represented or taught as means by which God’s grace is automatically conferred. This conforms to our commitment that God accomplishes His saving work in the means He has appointed in Scripture (WCF 21; WCF 27).
2.2 Format and placement. When used, the Stations of Reflection shall occur at a clearly announced point preceding the sermon so as to prepare hearts for the hearing and receiving of God’s Word. The segment shall run no longer than eight minutes and shall be conducted in an orderly manner so as not to distract from corporate worship.
2.3 Nature of objects and instruction. Four modest tables may be arranged as visual and mnemonic aids and shall be plainly described in the printed card at each station as symbolic prompts for prayer and Scripture meditation only. The objects used shall be simple and wholly symbolic (e.g., a lighted candle as a reminder of Christ, a small bowl of plain water as a reminder of baptism and cleansing in Christ, a small vessel of oil set aside for pastoral anointing upon request and not used as a public rite, and a card with a short Scriptural meditation). No object shall be labeled or presented as “holy water,” nor shall incense or other elements be used or presented as effecting grace. Instruction printed at each station shall explicitly say that these elements are symbols intended to focus prayer and reflection on Scripture, not to produce or “open” a heart to grace by virtue of touching or handling the objects.
2.4 Voluntariness. Participation is entirely voluntary; no communicant shall be required, pressured, or otherwise made to use or approach any station. All congregants and visitors shall be informed in the printed order and by announcement that participation is optional.
2.5 Pastoral anointing. Pastoral anointing with oil for the sick (James 5:14) may be offered through the Session’s pastoral ministry, but such anointing shall be private, by pastoral invitation or request, and not part of a corporate obligatory ritual. Any use of oil for this pastoral purpose shall be clearly pastoral and private, not a public rite or requirement.

Article III — Annual Covenant Renewal (Church Anniversary)
3.1 Purpose. On the church anniversary we shall observe a corporate time of covenant renewal and thanksgiving in which members may publicly reaffirm their trust in Christ and their commitment to the congregation’s gospel work. This observance shall be biblical in form and content and shall avoid rites or practices that imply that material acts have a sacramental efficacy not appointed by Scripture (WCF 21; larger catechism principles).
3.2 Form. The annual service shall include Scripture readings, corporate prayer, a congregational confession and assurance of pardon as appropriate, the singing of psalms and hymns, and an opportunity for the congregation to unite in a verbal covenant renewal or dedication to the Lord—phrased in biblically sound terms and approved by the Session in advance. The Session shall provide the form of words for the congregation to use, but any such corporate words shall be framed as vows or declarations of dedication, not as magical or liturgical “decrees” that attempt to bind unseen spiritual outcomes. No physical touching of oil, water, or other items shall be mandated as part of this corporate reaffirmation. If oil is present for pastoral anointing, its use shall be private and only at individual request as provided in 2.5.
3.3 Prohibition of binding-decree language. The Session prohibits any liturgical language or practice at the annual observance that claims to “bind” a coming year spiritually by virtue of words spoken or objects touched in the service (e.g., a public “decree” that binds the year to the Lord by ritual). The congregation may, however, adopt covenantal resolutions or commitments that are publicly read and privately affirmed, acknowledging that true efficacy belongs to God and is effected by His Word and Spirit alone.

Article IV — Preaching and Placement
4.1 Preaching central. The preached Word is the principal means of grace in public worship and shall be honored accordingly (WCF 21.6). The sermon shall be scheduled to fall in the final third of the ordinary 75‑minute service so that the congregation departs after having been fed by the public reading and exposition of Scripture.
4.2 Length. No sermon in an ordinary Sunday service shall exceed twenty‑five (25) minutes. Ministers shall plan expositions that are faithful to the text, clear, and within the allotted time. The Session recognizes that exceptional occasions (e.g., ordinations, installations, special teaching series) may require a different length; such exceptions must be approved by the Session in writing in advance.
4.3 Preaching content. Preaching shall be biblical, doctrinally sound, and consistent with the Westminster Standards subscribed to by this Session. Sermons are to call sinners to repentance and to magnify Christ’s saving work by grace through faith.

Article V — Singing and Music
5.1 Repertoire. The congregation’s sung worship shall be drawn from the Session‑approved psalter and hymnal list. No song shall be introduced or sung in public worship unless it has been approved by the Session for congregational use and found to be theologically consistent with our confession and edifying in content.
5.2 Order and rehearsal. Musical elements shall serve the Word and the sacraments. Accompanists and singers shall rehearse sufficiently so that musical offerings are orderly, reverent, and conducive to congregational participation.

Article VI — Session Oversight and Compliance
6.1 Administration. The Worship‑Planning Team shall implement these Standards and submit any proposed changes to the Session for approval. Any deviation from these Standards in particular services requires prior Session approval.
6.2 Education. The Session shall ensure that the congregation is instructed as to the theological reasons for these Standards, particularly the voluntary and non‑sacramental character of the Stations of Reflection and the biblical nature of the annual covenant renewal.
6.3 Enforcement. The Session shall address non‑compliance with pastoral sensitivity and with due process under our polity. Repeated or willful contravention of these Standards by leaders of worship shall be addressed by the Session and may result in withdrawal of authorization to lead public worship until remediation and assurance of conformity are given.

Conclusion and Effective Date
These Standards are adopted by the Session on [date], pursuant to our subscription to the Westminster Standards and our responsibility to regulate the worship of this congregation. They are effective for all Sunday services beginning on the first Sunday after adoption. The Session commits to periodic review of these provisions to ensure they continue to serve faithful, God‑glorifying worship in this congregation.

Signed,
On behalf of the Session,
[Name], Moderator
[Date]

The Partners’ Christian Operating Covenant
for [Name] Landscaping, LLC

Preamble
We, the undersigned, believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, enter this covenant before God and one another. Conforming to the biblical duties of stewardship, honesty, charity, and brotherly love (the same duties set forth and commended in the historic Reformed teaching summarized in the Westminster Standards), we bind our persons and our business practices to the terms below. Our aim is to glorify God in our business, guard one another from the love of money, and order the company so that our work and wealth serve the gospel and our neighbors.

This Covenant is intended to be a binding agreement among the Partners and to be attached as a governing addendum to the company’s LLC operating agreement. It may be amended only as provided in §12 below.

Definitions
- “Company” means [Name] Landscaping, LLC.
- “Partners” means the four undersigned owners and any person who is admitted as a partner under the Company’s operating agreement and who signs this Covenant.
- “Lowest-paid field crew wage” means the regular gross pay (hourly or monthly as paid in normal payroll) of the currently lowest-paid field crew member employed by the Company, measured at the time the salary decision is made.
- “Gospel work” means the local congregation, church planting and strengthening efforts, recognized Reformed or evangelical missions organizations, or charities approved by the Partners pursuant to §6.

Agreement
1. On Holding the Company’s Reserve Cash
1.1 We covenant that the Company’s reserve funds shall not be placed in any interest-bearing deposit, bond, mutual fund, investment vehicle, or other instrument intended to earn interest or investment return. The Company’s reserves shall be held only as cash equivalents that do not bear interest, in the manner agreed by the Partners (for example: non-interest-bearing demand deposit accounts, and/or securely-held cash on premises as the Partners unanimously elect).
1.2 The Partners acknowledge the Biblical warning against trusting in uncertain riches and the responsibility to put hope in God rather than in accruing wealth. Consistent with that conviction we will not treat the Company’s reserves as a source for speculative gain.
1.3 Procedures for custody and security of reserve cash (safe, insured deposit box, dual custody, periodic counts, and documented custody logs) will be established and approved by a majority of Partners and recorded in the Company’s books.

2. On Opportunistic Acquisition of Competitors’ Business
2.1 If a competing landscaping company, or a former partner or affiliate of ours, experiences severe financial distress and an opportunity arises to buy client lists, equipment, or to hire key crews at favorable terms, the Partner who first becomes aware of the opportunity shall promptly and fully disclose it to all Partners in writing.
2.2 No Partner shall pursue such an opportunity individually in a way that excludes the Company. Instead, the Partners shall consider pursuing the opportunity together. A decision to acquire, to hire, or to decline shall require approval by at least three Partners (a 3/4 majority) unless all Partners unanimously agree to a different threshold for that particular opportunity.
2.3 If Partners agree to proceed but the Company lacks sufficient cash, Partners may contribute capital pro rata or as otherwise agreed in writing. Any acquisition shall be made in the Company’s name unless the Partners unanimously agree in writing to another lawful arrangement.

3. On Books, Records, and Contracts
3.1 Each Partner shall keep honest, accurate, and timely company books and records and shall make them open to inspection by any other Partner on reasonable request. The Company will adopt standard bookkeeping and payroll practices and will hold monthly accounting reviews at which financial statements are presented.
3.2 The Company shall render to every subcontractor, supplier, and other contracting party exactly what is required by the contract with that party—no less, no more. Claims, disputes, or corrections shall be handled promptly, honestly, and in accordance with the contract and applicable law.
3.3 Intentional concealment, falsification, or misrepresentation in the Company’s books is a material breach of this Covenant and shall give rise to remedial actions in §9.

4. On Partner Compensation and Proof of Heart
4.1 No Partner shall receive a salary greater than the current lowest-paid field crew wage except as provided in §4.2. Salaries paid to Partners for work performed shall be transparent and recorded in payroll.
4.2 A Partner who seeks to draw a salary higher than the lowest-paid field crew wage must first (a) request approval from the other Partners, and (b) spend in full one consecutive calendar month living on the crew wage (the “Proof Month”), demonstrating by accounting and testimony that he or she has actually lived on that amount. The Partners shall verify completion of the Proof Month before approving any higher salary.
4.3 Approval for a higher salary after the Proof Month shall require the written consent of at least three Partners, who shall judge whether the Partner’s conduct and testimony show freedom from covetousness and a godly motive for the higher pay.
4.4 Nothing in this section prevents distribution of profit in accordance with §5 after the fixed share for gospel work is set aside.

5. On Priority Giving for Gospel Work
5.1 Before any Partner receives a distribution of profit, the Company will set aside a fixed share of distributable profits for gospel work. The fixed share shall be 10% (one-tenth) of the Company’s distributable profit for each accounting period unless the Partners unanimously agree in writing to a different fixed percentage.
5.2 Recipients of the gospel share shall be approved by majority vote of the Partners, with priority given to the local congregation(s) of one or more Partners and to mission projects affirmed by the Partners. Disbursement shall be prompt and accompanied by a written statement describing the recipients and purpose.
5.3 This giving is an essential part of our stewardship and is to be done cheerfully, transparently, and as an example to our employees and neighbors.

6. On Conduct Toward Competitors and Former Partners
6.1 Partners shall not speak evil of, disparage, or otherwise badmouth a competitor or a former Partner for the purpose of winning bids or obtaining business. The Company’s marketing and bidding shall be conducted on truthfulness, the quality of workmanship, and integrity.
6.2 If a Partner violates §6.1, the Partner shall, at minimum, (a) issue a written apology, (b) make restitution for any direct, provable harm caused, and (c) submit to remedial measures in §9. Repeated or egregious violations may trigger the buyout procedure in §10.

7. On Employees and Wages
7.1 We covenant to pay employees justly and to treat them with dignity. Wages, benefits, safety, and lawful treatment are matters of conscience and central to our witness; we will comply with all applicable employment laws and will endeavor to exceed the bare minimum where the Company’s resources allow.

8. On Conflict Resolution and Discipline
8.1 Partners shall first seek to resolve disputes among themselves in a spirit of humility and love, consulting Scripture and prayer.
8.2 If a dispute cannot be resolved informally within 30 days, the Partners will submit the matter to Christian mediation by an impartial pair of mature Christians agreed by the Partners (for example, elders from a local congregation unaffiliated with the Company). If mediation fails, the Partners agree to binding arbitration before a Christian arbitrator or panel agreed by the Partners or, if none can be agreed, appointed pursuant to [insert agreed selection method].
8.3 Where a Partner’s conduct is willfully contrary to this Covenant, the Company may impose sanctions including (but not limited to) temporary suspension of profit distributions to that Partner, requirement of restitution, loss of voting rights for a stated period, or other measures proportionate to the breach. Severe or unrepentant breach may lead to buyout under §10.

9. On Remedies for Material Breach
9.1 A material breach of §§1, 3, 4, 5, or 6 is subject to remedial measures described in §8 and §10. Restitution and compensation shall follow biblical principles of making right wrongs and restoring relationships, to the extent this is reasonably possible.
9.2 The injured party’s rights at law or equity are preserved, provided Partners first exhaust the internal disciplinary and arbitration procedures herein. Nothing in this Covenant is intended to waive mandatory legal protections for third parties or employees.

10. On Buyout and Withdrawal
10.1 If a Partner is to be bought out (whether by voluntary withdrawal, by reason of unrepentant breach, disability, death, or other cause), the price and process shall follow the Company’s operating agreement. In the absence of specific provision there, the Partners agree to obtain an independent business valuation from a mutually agreed appraiser and to effect a buyout using that valuation within 90 days on terms to be agreed; if terms cannot be agreed, the arbitration process in §8.2 will set fair terms.
10.2 A Partner whose conduct necessitates buyout under this Covenant (for example, repeated willful violation of §6.1 or concealment of funds under §3) may forfeit certain agreed premiums or face valuation adjustments as determined by binding arbitration.

11. On Public Profession and Witness
11.1 We will maintain a public and private witness consistent with the gospel: honesty in advertising and bids, faithfulness in performance, and care for customers and employees.
11.2 We agree to teach and encourage workers under our supervision in sound ethical work principles consistent with our faith, while respecting each worker’s conscience and legal protections.

12. On Amendment and Duration
12.1 This Covenant is entered into voluntarily and shall remain in force so long as the Company exists or until amended or abrogated in writing by the unanimous written consent of all Partners.
12.2 Any amendment must be reduced to writing, signed by all Partners, and attached to the Company’s operating agreement.

13. Conscience, Church Discipline, and the Westminster Standards
13.1 We covenant to act in a manner consistent with Scripture and with the Christian creeds and confessions we hold dear. We do not intend this Covenant to supplant church discipline, but to reflect the same biblical convictions about stewardship, honesty, and charity taught in the Scriptures and summarized in the historic Reformed standards.

TEAM CULTURE & CONDUCT CODE — Community Youth Soccer (Co‑ed, ages 13–16)

Our purpose
We play to develop skill, teamwork, and character. This team is inspired by Christian convictions about honesty, respect, self‑control, and loving our neighbor, but participation is open to all players in the community. We will treat one another and opponents with dignity, play hard but fairly, and protect the safety and wellbeing of every player.

Acknowledgement
All players and a parent/guardian must sign this Code of Conduct as a condition of participation. Signing indicates you have read it, agree to the expectations, and understand the coach will enforce it fairly.

Core expectations (binding)
1. Respect and sportsmanship
- Players will treat referees, coaches, opponents, teammates, volunteers, and families with respect at all times. Abusive, hateful, or harassing language or conduct is not permitted and may lead to disciplinary action, up to removal from the team.
- We honor referees’ calls. Disputes are resolved respectfully and through proper channels, not by public shaming or social‑media campaigns.

2. Punctuality and preparedness
- Players will arrive on time for practices and games, ready to participate.
- If a player will be late or absent, a parent or player must notify the coach in advance.

3. Uniforms and appropriate athletic attire
- Players are expected to wear the league uniform for games and appropriate, safe athletic clothing at practices.
- “Appropriate” means clothing that allows safe play (e.g., athletic shorts or skorts, shirts with sleeves or secure straps, shin guards, no jewelry that poses a hazard). The coach will provide guidance if an item is unsafe for play.
- This standard applies equally to all players regardless of gender; we will not single out or police one gender more stringently than another.
- If a player cannot afford a uniform or proper gear, they will not be shamed, benched, or disciplined for that reason. The coach will work discreetly with the family to provide help (loaner gear, assistance funds, or community resources).

4. Travel and supervision (carpools)
- Players must travel to and from official team events with a parent/guardian or with a driver for whom the parent/guardian has given written permission.
- Parents should inform the coach in advance whenever their child will be riding with another adult. For the safety and comfort of minors, carpools should be pre‑arranged and transparent; parents may choose same‑gender carpools but the coach will not require gender‑segregated transport.
- If the league or local authorities have specific transport/supervision rules, those rules will be followed.

5. Music, team environment, and optional devotional activities
- Practices and team events are family environments. The coach will select any background music to be family‑friendly and appropriate for athletic focus.
- The team will offer optional, short, voluntary devotional moments (prayer, Scripture reading, or Bible study) before or after practice/games for those who wish to participate. Participation is voluntary and requires parental consent for minors; players will never be required to join religious activities as a condition of playing.

6. Playing time, captains, and selection decisions
- Playing time and captainship are coach decisions and will be awarded based on transparent criteria: attendance, attitude, effort, teamwork, sportsmanship, and demonstrated skill.
- There will be no special allocation of playing time, captaincy, or other on‑field advantages in exchange for financial support, donations, or external influence. Commitment may be recognized, but preferential treatment for specific families (including promises to “always play” particular players or deliberately prioritize donors’ children) is prohibited.

7. Discipline and enforcement
- Minor violations: private coach‑player conversation and/or parent notification, followed by corrective expectations.
- Repeated or serious violations (bullying, violent conduct, discrimination, or endangering others): progressive discipline that can include suspension or removal from the team.
- All discipline will be handled without public shaming. Parents may request a private meeting to discuss discipline decisions. If unresolved, escalate to the team committee.

8. Communication and conflict resolution
- Parents should bring concerns directly to the coach first and avoid campaigning through team group chats, social media, or by organizing parents against specific players/families or the coach.
- Steps: 1) Speak privately to the coach; 2) If unresolved, request a meeting with the coach and program coordinator; 3) If still unresolved, bring the concern to the team committee per committee procedures.

9. Inclusion and non‑discrimination
- This team will not discriminate against any player for financial hardship, race, gender, religion, or family status.
- We will protect the safety and dignity of all players and abide by league and civil laws regarding minors and discrimination.

- Transparent criteria for playing time and captain selection: Keeps the process fair and limits the appearance or reality of favoritism.

What I WILL NOT include (and why)
- I will not require a religious “purity pledge” as a condition of team membership. Requiring a personal religious pledge or confession to play crosses from coaching into private conscience matters and excludes those of other convictions. I will instead offer optional, voluntary devotional opportunities and encourage personal integrity and purity as part of character formation.

- I will not ban all “secular music” at practice as a categorical rule. I will require that any music played be family‑friendly and appropriate for practice; explicitly sexual, profane, or divisive material is not allowed. This balances pastoral conviction with appropriate oversight and respects families’ varied backgrounds.
- I will not permit or write into policy any clause that channels guaranteed playing time, captaincy, or hidden preferential treatment to particular families in exchange for donations or influence. That undermines fairness and the integrity of the program.

Theological and pastoral rationale (brief)
My discernment is shaped by the Westminster Standards’ clear emphasis that true religion is heart‑based and that Christians are obliged to live honorably before God and neighbor. The Standards warn against enforcing external rites or human inventions as necessary for spiritual standing. In practice, that means we may teach and model Christian virtues (honesty, purity, self‑control, love), and offer voluntary spiritual means (prayer, Scripture), but we must not coerce conscience or make outward rituals the price of community participation. At the same time, the Standards call for civil order, charity, and the care of the weak — so I must preserve safety rules, fair governance, and protect those who lack material means. This balance — sincere spiritual formation without coercion, coupled with fairness and care — is what I will implement in the Code.

Sacred Arts Policy
(for adoption by Session — applicable to all visual elements in church property and in the gathered worship)

Preamble
We adopt this policy to govern the use of visual arts in the life and buildings of our congregation under the authority of Scripture interpreted by the Westminster Standards to which this Session and congregation subscribe. Our aim is pastoral: to glorify God, to guard the purity of worship, to nurture the flock in sound doctrine, and to avoid superstition and idolatry. Where the Standards are explicit we apply them strictly; where faithful Christians have differed, we state honestly our chosen practice and the reason for it.

Definitions and guiding principles
- “Visual element” = any painting, photograph, banner, projection, architectural ornament, book illustration, flannelgraph figure, printed text or framed document, or any other pictorial or material display on church property or used in the gathered service.
- We apply the Second Commandment’s prohibition of images used in religious veneration and the Westminster teaching that worship must be regulated by Scripture; therefore we will not use images as objects of worship or veneration, nor permit anything in the worship setting that functions as a substitute for the Word and sacraments.
- The “means of grace” are the ordinary channels God has appointed to convey His covenant blessing (the preached Word, the sacraments, prayer, etc.). Visual elements are not, and will never be presented as, means of grace.
- The Session is the final authority for what visual elements are permitted in our buildings and in our gathered services.

Policy (binding rules and specific rulings)

1) Portrait of Jesus as centerpiece over the communion table
Decision: Not permitted.
Rationale: The Westminster standards require that worship be free from images or representations that might be objects of reverence or focal points for worship. A large, realistic painted portrait presented as a focal point over the Lord’s Table would present a material depiction of the incarnate Son in a context where the assembly is to center upon the Word and the sacrament instituted by Christ. That creates a real risk of veneration of an image and confusion about where Christ’s presence is to be found under Scripture’s appointed means. Therefore requests to hang any portrait (realistic or stylized) of Jesus above or immediately as the focal ornament of the communion table will be refused.

2) Blanket ban on all visual art in the building
Decision: Not adopted.
Rationale and limits: While the Westminster tradition is strongly iconoclastic with respect to images of God used in worship, the Standards do not require a categorical prohibition of every visual element everywhere. There is room in faithful practice for the careful use of visual media for instruction, pastoral care, and lawful decorative expression so long as such media are not objects of worship, do not depict God or the persons of the Trinity in a way that invites veneration, and are not presented as conveying grace apart from the Word and sacraments. The insistence that “thou shalt not make any likeness” forbids making images for the purposes of religious worship and veneration; it does not, in our judgment, require forbidding all pictures in every context (e.g., educational materials, historical displays, tasteful architecture) on church property. Because conscience and pastoral prudence vary, the Session will exercise oversight as described below.

3) Children’s ministry illustrated storybooks and flannelgraph figures of Jesus and the disciples
Decision: Permitted, with safeguards.
Rationale: The Standards affirm the importance of instructing the young in Scripture and the catechism. Use of simple, clearly instructional illustrations in children’s classrooms that depict biblical persons for the purpose of narrative teaching is allowable so long as (a) such materials are kept in the children’s ministry spaces (not installed as devotional imagery in the sanctuary or above sacramental fixtures), (b) teachers explicitly present them as pedagogical aids and not as objects of reverence, and (c) the depictions are simple and not used to foster imaginative worship of an image. Flannelgraph or simple drawn figures used in Sunday school and children’s worship are therefore allowed under Session oversight.

4) Projected abstract, non-figurative imagery during congregational singing
Decision: Permitted, with Session approval and guidelines.
Rationale: Abstract light, color, and moving textures that do not depict the persons of the Godhead, biblical scenes, or saints, and that are used to support a worshipful atmosphere, are not intrinsically forbidden by the Standards so long as they are never presented as objects of devotion or as a means of grace. Because the Second Commandment’s force concerns likenesses for worship and veneration rather than purely abstract aesthetic elements, such projections may be used when approved in advance by the Session and when accompanied by pastoral guidance that the congregation’s focus remains on the Word, prayer, and sacraments.

5) Framed printed Scripture texts and the confession in the entryway
Decision: Permitted and commended.
Rationale: The Westminster Standards place Scripture at the center of the church’s life. Framed Scripture passages and our historic confession displayed in public areas for instruction and orientation are consistent with confessional piety and public catechesis. They must be presented reverently but not in a way that treats the physical object as an object of worship. Display of these texts is encouraged as a means of instructing and reminding members and visitors of our doctrinal commitments.

6) Session approval for all visual elements and prohibition of presenting visual elements as means of grace
Decision: Firm requirement.
Rationale and procedure: Any visual element used in the gathered service or permanently placed in the sanctuary shall require prior approval by the Session (or by a Session-appointed arts subcommittee acting under clear written authority). Visual elements shall never be presented as a “means of grace” alongside preaching, the sacraments, and prayer. When controversy or conscience objections arise, the Session will hear the parties, weigh the matter according to Scripture and our Standards, and make a binding determination for the congregation.

Implementation and governance
- Arts Review: The Session shall appoint an Arts Review Subcommittee (ministry staff member from arts, two elders appointed by Session, and one pastoral staff) to review proposals, ensure theological conformity to this policy, and make recommendations to Session. No permanent installation or use in the gathered service may proceed without Session approval.
- Placement: Sanctuary focal points that affect congregational attention (behind the pulpit, over the communion table, on the chancel wall) are subject to the strictest restraint: no images portraying the persons of the Trinity or Christ’s visage as an object of devotion shall be placed there.
- Educational use: Materials for teaching, children’s ministry, study rooms, and exhibit areas may include illustrations and photographs provided they are clearly pedagogical, not used for devotion, and approved by the Arts Review Subcommittee.
- Review and pastoral discretion: The Session will exercise pastoral sensitivity to conscience and local practice, recognizing where faithful Christians may differ. When in doubt, prioritize safeguarding worship from anything that might become an icon or a substitute for the Word and sacraments.
- Annual review: This policy will be reviewed annually by Session to address new media or unforeseen pastoral issues.

Honest notes about contested matters
- The strictest iconoclast position—banning all images in every space on the theory that any likeness is forbidden in any setting—is a faithful, historically Reformed option held by some. The Westminster Standards, however, historically and practically have allowed exercise of pastoral judgment over images used for instruction and decoration so long as they are not used in worship. Because reasonable, God-fearing Christians differ about edge cases, Session must govern on the side of pastoral prudence while also allowing lawful uses that aid instruction and do not risk idolatry.
- The use of imagery that depicts Christ’s human face is particularly sensitive because it most readily tempts veneration; thus this policy forbids such imagery as a focal point in worship spaces (especially over the Lord’s Table), while allowing restricted, pedagogical depictions in non-worship classroom contexts under Session oversight.

Conclusion and final authority
This policy is to be read under the authority of Scripture and the Westminster Standards to which we subscribe. The Session is the final judge in its application consistent with the pastoral and theological principles stated above. All ministry leaders, volunteers, and donors are asked to abide by this policy and to bring proposed visual materials to the Arts Review Subcommittee before public use or placement.

Preamble — a covenantal framing
We, the undersigned, who are brothers and sisters in Christ and members of this personal-finance fellowship, enter this Contentment Covenant before God, trusting in His providence and seeking to walk in the practical holiness urged by Scripture and the Reformed tradition. In the spirit of the Westminster Confession and Catechisms — which call God sovereign over all things, press believers to trust Him for daily provision, require mercy and stewardship toward the poor, and commend mutual exhortation and discipline among the faithful — we bind ourselves to one another in love, honesty, and accountability. Our aim is not mere rule-keeping but gospel-shaped sanctification: to grow in contentment, to rejoice at one another’s good, and to steward God’s gifts to the glory of Christ.

By this covenant we willingly submit ourselves to the commitments below, to be held accountable to one another before the Lord.

I. Core commitments (to be observed in practice and tracked publicly in our group records)
1. Giving: Each member commits to give at least ten percent (10%) of their gross income to the local church or to explicit gospel work (missions, church planting, direct evangelistic ministry). Gifts shall be recorded in the group’s shared giving sheet each month, and members agree to furnish necessary evidence of giving on request for the sake of mutual accountability and encouragement.

2. Major purchases above the median: No member shall purchase a home, automobile, or take a vacation whose total cost exceeds the current group median for that category without first bringing the proposed purchase to the group in our monthly meeting and securing the group’s counsel and approval. The purpose of this rule is mutual discernment about stewardship and to guard against competing lifestyles that foster envy or pride.

3. Envy and rejoicing: We covenant to cultivate gratitude and to rejoice genuinely when a fellow member prospers. If a member becomes aware of envy, covetousness, or resentful desire toward a brother or sister in the group, that member will confess that heart-state to the group at the next regular meeting (or to their accountability partner that week) so that we might pray, counsel, and restore joy together.

4. Limits on pursuit of additional income: Believing that anxious acquisitiveness fosters discontent, members covenant not to pursue raises, promotions, or a second income stream for the sake of greater affluence, status, or accumulation. (See Clarifications and Exceptions below.)

5. “Enough” journal: Each member will keep a monthly “Enough” journal listing what they already have — spiritual and material blessings, relationships, means, and recurring needs — and reflecting briefly on gratefulness and sufficiency. The journal will be reviewed monthly by the member’s accountability partner, who will pray with them and give honest encouragement toward contentment.

6. Open budgets each month: We will meet monthly and open our household budgets to one another for honest counsel, prayer, and mutual exhortation. Openness will include income, regular expenditures, charitable giving, and planned significant purchases. Members pledge to receive counsel in humility and to offer it in gentleness and truth.

II. Mutual responsibilities and process
- Accountability partners: Each member will have an accountability partner chosen by mutual consent. Partners meet (in person or by phone) monthly to review the “Enough” journal, discuss temptations to covetousness, confess struggles, and pray.

- Confidentiality and pastoral use: What is confessed in the group is treated as confidential among members, except where there is ongoing unrepentant breach of the covenant that requires group intervention, or where civil law (harm to self/others, abuse, illegal activity) requires disclosure.

- Counsel and restoration: When a member is found to be in breach, we shall follow steps of loving correction: private admonition by an accountability partner; if unrepentant, private admonition by two or three members; public admonition in the monthly meeting with a call to repentance; and, if necessary, suspension or removal from the fellowship until genuine repentance is evident. Discipline will be exercised humbly, patiently, and always with a view to restoration.

III. Clarifications and exceptions (to preserve biblical balance and conscience)
- On earning and provision: The Westminster Standards affirm the lawfulness of lawful labor and provision for one’s family. Accordingly, this covenant is not intended to forbid the faithful fulfillment of responsibilities to spouse, children, or dependents, nor to prohibit vocational advancement that is necessary for honest provision, greater service to family, or increasing one’s ability to give and serve the gospel. The specific commitment in section I.4 is aimed at refraining from active pursuits of more income for reasons of status, luxury, or acquisitiveness. Members facing legitimate vocational decisions (e.g., a promotion required to support dependents, or a second job temporarily necessary in a season of need) will bring the matter to their accountability partner and the group for counsel and prayer rather than simply concealing the change.

- On emergencies and seasonality: Temporary exceptions (e.g., necessary purchases for safety, health, or urgent family need) may be approved by one’s accountability partner and reported to the group at the next meeting.

IV. Practical records and administration
- The group will maintain a shared electronic sheet for: (a) recording monthly givings to church/gospel work; (b) listing current medians for home, car, vacation cost categories; and (c) tracking adherence to meeting attendance, journal submission, and accountability partner meetings.

- Each member will supply their accountability partner’s name to the group administrator and will sign the shared sheet as a statement of intent to comply.

V. Signatures and commitment
We pledge, before God and one another, to live under this covenant, praying that the Holy Spirit would work in us the grace of contentment, generosity, humility, and mutual love. We submit our finances, our desires, our joys, and our struggles to Christ’s lordship and to the wise counsel of this fellowship.

Preamble — Covenant and Purpose
We are a gospel household: bound together not merely by convenience but by covenant. We live together to encourage one another toward holiness, mutual care, and joyful obedience to Christ. This Rule of Life is offered in that spirit — warm in charity, sober in seriousness — and is grounded in Scripture’s call to contentment, stewardship, mutual accountability, and holy living. It is also framed in the convictions of the Reformed covenantal tradition (as taught in the Westminster standards): as a gathered Christian people we submit ourselves under God’s word and under the loving oversight of appointed leaders for the sake of sanctification and right order.

By signing below each resident affirms that they enter into this covenant voluntarily, will submit to its requirements in good faith, and accept the house leaders’ responsibility to enforce it in love and with a view toward repentance and restoration.

Core Commitments (required, enforceable)
1) Worship and Gathering
- Each resident will attend the house’s Sunday gathering and Wednesday gathering in person unless excused in advance for serious reasons (illness, work conflict approved by a leader, or other urgent necessity).
- Absences without prior notice or a legitimate reason will be treated seriously and addressed by leaders.

Rationale: We gather to be formed as the body of Christ, to receive Word and sacrament, and to practice mutual encouragement.

2) Financial Limitation (monthly cap)
- No resident may earn, save, or spend beyond the monthly cap set by the house leaders. The leaders will announce the cap in writing at the beginning of each month.
- Any plan to pursue additional income (a raise in existing employment, a second job, freelance/side income, selling goods for profit, etc.) must receive prior written approval from the leaders.
- Rationale statement to residents: “The contented heart doesn’t need more.” We practice voluntary limits to train hearts away from covetousness; ambition for more may become the root of covetousness and undermine our common life.

3) Financial Transparency and Community Discernment
- All residents will keep their personal and shared expenditures recorded on the shared house budget spreadsheet, visible to all housemates at all times.
- Any single purchase over $40 (personal or shared) must be posted to the house channel with a short explanation and left open for the group to weigh in before the purchase is completed. In urgent cases post immediately afterward with explanation.
- Leaders maintain an administrative column to record approvals and notes.
- Rationale: We “kill covetousness in community” by practicing mutual transparency and prudence.

4) Shared Chores and Common Meal Fund
- Residents will contribute to agreed household chores (schedule to be posted) and participate in preparation/clean-up for the common meals.
- Each resident will contribute to the common meal fund at the rate and cadence set by the leaders; this fund’s balance is tracked on the shared spreadsheet.
- Failure to perform assigned chores or to make meal-fund contributions is subject to corrective steps by leaders.

5) Mobility and Major Employment Changes
- Residents may not accept a job offer in another city or otherwise permanently relocate without a written release signed by the house leaders.
- If a resident is considering relocation, they must first meet with the leaders, present the opportunity, and request a release. Leaders will normally grant release if there is clear godly necessity, provision for faithful departure, and no unresolved issues in the covenant relationship. The resident must ordinarily give at least 30 days’ notice unless otherwise agreed.
- Rationale: “Discontentment always disguises itself as opportunity.” The house exercises care to discern genuine vocation from restless discontent that would fracture covenant life.

Procedures, Oversight, and Requests
- The house leaders (appointed elders/stewards) bear responsibility for administering this Rule. They will publish the monthly financial cap and any procedural forms (request templates, budget spreadsheet location, etc.).
- Requests for earning/saving/spending beyond the cap, for side-income approval, or for release to relocate must be submitted in writing (email or house channel) with a clear purpose and anticipated financial figures. Leaders will respond within seven calendar days; in complicated cases they may request a short meeting.
- Appeals: A resident may appeal a leader decision to the house’s elder-review panel (the leaders plus one external advisor acceptable to resident and leaders) within 7 days of the decision. The panel will seek a timely, charitable resolution.

Consequences and Restoration
- First breach: private pastoral meeting with leaders; explanation and plan for restitution/repair where applicable.
- Second breach: formal probation (30 days) with a written restoration plan (including missed contributions, repayment of excess funds, or renewed commitment to gatherings and chores).

Short answer up front

- Streaming the service to shut‑ins: lawful and allowable under the Standards; it is a pastoral/disciplinary question for the session to regulate, but an elder may not forbid a lawful means of worship or mercy on merely private, non‑biblical scruple. The session may set policies about how screens/cameras are used so worship remains “decent and in order” (WCF 21) and to avoid anything that would be “will‑worship.”

- “Virtual Lord’s Supper” (people at home eating their own elements while the pastor speaks over a camera): not a lawful administration of the sacrament under the Westminster Standards. The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament to be duly administered by Christ’s ordinance through the church’s ministry and received by the people as a visible, outward sign and seal; it may not be converted into remote private self‑administration by means of a stream or video.

Reasoning and references to the Standards

1) Streaming the service to shut‑ins
- The Westminster Confession treats public worship as an ordinary duty of the church that is to be performed “in the public congregation” but insists worship be “decently and in order” and not by “will‑worship” (WCF ch. 21). Technology (cameras, screens, streaming) is not an element of worship instituted by Christ; it is an outward circumstance or aid.
- The Confession recognizes that things not commanded in Scripture are not to be imposed as necessary worship (again WCF 21 on rites and ceremonies), and elsewhere affirms the proper exercise of Christian liberty in things indifferent to God’s law. Using technology to bring the preaching, prayer, sacraments (for viewing) and singing to those unable to attend is a lawful pastoral means to extend ministry and mercy.
- That said, the session has responsibility for the order of worship and may regulate how technology is used so that worship remains reverent and faithful to Scripture and the Standards. An individual elder’s insistence on tearing out cameras on the ground that they are “worldly devices” is a private judgment; to forbid a lawful practice across the congregation without Scriptural warrant would be inappropriate under the Confession’s teaching about worship and Christian liberty.

Practical session guidance: adopt rules that permit streaming for shut‑ins and others who legitimately cannot attend, but require oversight (who operates cameras, what is shown, respectful placement, no distracting screens in the chancel, recorded services archived appropriately). If an elder objects on conscience, the session should hear him, but not treat a personal scruple as a binding order for the whole church absent biblical warrant.

2) “Virtual Lord’s Supper”
- The Westminster Confession’s teaching on the Lord’s Supper (WCF ch. 30) insists the supper is a sacrament instituted by Christ to be observed by the church. The outward elements (bread and wine) are signs and seals given under the ministry of the church. The sacrament is not a mere private devotion but an ordinance of Christ to be administered and received within the visible church by the officers appointed to that ministry.
- The sacrament’s efficacy is not in the mere utterance of words or in imagery but in the covenantal sign and seal administered by Christ’s appointed means. Reducing the supper to dispersed persons eating privately at home while a minister speaks over a camera collapses the sacramental administration into private self‑administration and removes the visible, ordained ministry and the congregation’s common participation that the Standards presuppose.
- For these reasons, the Westminster Standards do not support calling a streamed, remote, self‑served act “the Lord’s Supper.” That cannot be treated as the sacrament’s lawful administration. At best, people watching may be invited to spiritual communion/devotional meditation (which is pastoral care for those who cannot attend), but that must be explicitly distinguished from receiving the sacrament.

Pastoral and practical alternatives consistent with the Standards
- Continue streaming the service for shut‑ins for preaching and prayer, but make clear online viewers are not receiving the Lord’s Supper through the stream.
- Where there is genuine necessity (sickness, infirmity, imprisonment), the Standards recognize the church’s responsibility to minister the sacraments pastorally. The normal and preferred way is for an ordained minister (sometimes with an elder) to go to shut‑ins and administer the elements personally (with due care). The session should make provision for such pastoral visits and administration.
- Provide spiritual‑communion guidance for online viewers (encourage personal prayer, meditation on Christ’s sacrifice, longing to receive the sacrament, etc.) but do not baptize those practices with sacramental language.
- Require that any changes to sacramental practice be decided by the session (and, where needed, presbytery) in keeping with Presbyterian order and the Standards; ministers do not have liberty to unilaterally change the outward administration of sacraments.

Suggested session ruling language (concise)
1. Streaming of the services for shut‑ins and the infirm is permitted as a lawful pastoral means of extending preaching, prayer, and praise, subject to session oversight to ensure decency and order in worship.
2. A streamed “virtual Lord’s Supper,” in which dispersed persons eat and drink private elements at home in response to words spoken over a camera, is not a lawful administration of the sacrament under the Westminster Standards and therefore is not permitted. The session will make provision for pastoral, in‑person administration to those who by necessity cannot attend.

I will lead this as a binding, covenant order for our house-church. We adopt it together, keep it weekly, and hold one another accountable in love and according to Scripture and the church’s discipline as taught in the Reformed (Westminster) tradition: public worship is a duty of Christians, prayer for the sick is Scriptural, and the church may exercise loving discipline when members deliberately neglect their covenantal obligations.

Order of Gathering (weekly; binding covenant)

Preamble
- We covenant, before God and one another, to gather weekly as a household of Christ, to worship, to bear one another’s burdens, and to practice holy discipline for mutual growth and faithfulness. We do so in humility, under the authority of Scripture, and with pastoral care for one another’s conscience and welfare.

Weekly Order
1) Opening
- We open with a psalm or hymn led by whoever is appointed, followed by a short prayer of praise and dependence on God. (Scriptural pattern: psalmody, prayer.)

2) Reading and Brief Teaching
- One member reads the appointed passage aloud and gives a brief, plain exposition (5–15 minutes) that points to Christ, calls for repentance, and applies Scripture to life. We rotate who reads/teaches on a published roster.

3) Prayer for the Sick / Anointing
- Anyone who is sick or asks for prayer may come forward. We will anoint with oil from our designated “healing jar,” lay hands on the person, and pray, confidently pleading God’s promise to hear and, as He wills, to heal (James 5:14–15; Matt. 18:19–20). The anointing is an act of worship and pleading faith, not a magical talisman; we do not require abandonment of medical care — members are urged to seek appropriate medical attention and not regard anointing as a substitute for necessary treatment.
- The jar: we keep one designated “healing jar” of oil for these acts. Keeping the jar filled and using it weekly is part of our covenant practice and discipline: it is the sign and observable habit that binds our fellowship to this ministry of prayer. The households covenant to maintain and use the jar as described below; persistent, deliberate neglect of this covenantal practice will be treated as a breach of our fellowship commitments (see Discipline, below).

4) Attendance and Accountability
- Every household covenants to attend the weekly gathering. No household may miss a weekly gathering for any reason short of hospitalization. A missed week without the hospitalization excuse is treated as a breach of covenant — a sin against the body — and is to be confessed publicly at the next gathering (see Discipline, below). If a household anticipates unavoidable absence due to hospitalization, they must inform the eldership/appointed elder promptly and provide any possible notice.
- Emergencies that truly prevent attendance (hospitalization, incapacitating illness) excuse the absence; such cases are handled pastorally. We expect reasonable documentation when needed for the good order of the church.

5) Offering for One Another’s Needs
- We take up a freewill offering at each meeting for members’ needs (and for mercy and mission as directed by the congregation). The offering is shared according to need and according to the judgment of the appointed stewards and elders. All financial handling is to be transparent to the fellowship.

6) Shared Common Meal
- We close by sharing a common meal together as a household of hospitality and mutual care. This is distinct from the Lord’s Supper unless expressly celebrated as such; we will observe the Lord’s Supper according to our established practice when appointed. The common meal is to be ready and shared in a spirit of thanksgiving, bearing one another’s dietary needs in mind.

Practical Details and Roles
- Rotating Ministry Roster: A weekly schedule lists who opens the meeting (psalm/hymn & prayer), who reads/teaches, who prepares the meal, who is steward of the healing jar, and who receives the offering. Rosters are published monthly.
- Healing Jar Steward: A household is appointed in rotation to ensure the jar remains filled with olive oil (or suitable oil) and available each week. If the appointed steward cannot fill the jar, they must arrange a replacement before the meeting.
- Record of Attendance: A confidential attendance register is kept to support faithful accountability and care; it is not for public exposure outside the fellowship except as required by law.
- Confidential Care: Pastoral visits, medical referrals, and private counseling are provided for those who need help beyond the public meeting.

Discipline, Confession, and Restoration
- We follow the biblical, pastoral pattern of admonition and restoration. If a household misses a meeting without hospitalization, that unexcused absence is treated as a breach of our covenant. The process is:
  1) On the next weekly meeting the household will make a public confession before the gathered body, expressing repentance and likelihood of amendment. The confession is brief, humble, and aimed at restoration, not public shaming.
  2) Pastors/elders will follow up in pastoral counsel to ensure the causes of absence are addressed and to help restore the household to faithful attendance.
  3) Repeated unrepentant neglect will be handled according to our church discipline procedures: private admonition, then public rebuke, and, as a last resort, exclusion from fellowship until repentance (see our discipline covenant).
- We emphasize gentleness, patience, and a goal of restoration; confession is for repentance and reconciliation, not for spectacle.

Theological and Pastoral Clarifications (to prevent superstition and harm)
- The practices above are Scripture-based expressions of worship and mutual care (assembly, prayer for the sick, almsgiving, common table). We affirm that such practices are means of grace and signs of our covenant, but we deny that the jar, oil, or any ritual has automatic, mechanical power apart from God’s sovereign mercy. Any teaching that makes the jar or weekly use into a talisman or that would bar someone from God’s covenant because of an occasional lapse is forbidden.
- Medical care is to be sought when needed. No member is to be counseled to refuse necessary medical treatment. The anointing with oil is prayerful dependence on God in concert with wisdom and means.

Short answer up front: I cannot, in good conscience and consistent with the Westminster Standards to which I subscribe, draft or bind the congregation to the exact provisions you wrote — particularly items (2), (3), and (5) as stated. Those provisions introduce innovations in worship and impose coerced external acts and private-public confession practices that the Confession and Catechisms do not authorize.
