Why I cannot adopt the requested clauses as written
- The Westminster Confession teaches the regulative principle of worship: the acceptable way of worshipping God is instituted by Him and is to be directed by His Word (WCF, “Of Religious Worship”). Elements, gestures, and rites of the public worship of God must be appointed in Scripture; innovations not instituted by Christ are to be avoided. Making an “activation” block the appointed channel through which renewing grace comes elevates a created practice into a required sacramental channel not found in Scripture.
- The Standards also require that church discipline and pastoral correction be conducted according to Scripture (see WCF “Of Church Censures” and the Catechisms’ teaching on repentance and confession). Compelling physical behavior (falling backward on touch), labeling a member “resisting the flow,” or requiring monthly public confession of private affections (jealousy) would violate the conscience and liberty of the believer and risk injuring the church’s worship and charity. The Standards distinguish private confession to God and pastoral/private confession for help from public confession required only for scandalous sins (not every jealous thought).

Because of those commitments, I will not draft or sign a covenant that binds members to the specific compulsory practices you listed in (2), (3), and (5). I will, however, propose the following covenant that is warm, binding, orderly, and faithful to both the desire for renewal and the Westminster Standards.

Worship Renewal Covenant of [Church Name]
Preamble
We, the members of [Church Name], united under Christ and submitted to Holy Scripture, desire that our corporate worship glorify God, build up the body of Christ, protect the consciences of believers, and minister grace and mercy to one another according to the Word. To that end, and under the oversight of the Session, we enter this binding Worship Renewal Covenant.

Article I — Time, Order, and Duration
1. The Lord’s Day public worship service shall begin at 10:00 a.m. sharp, shall follow the printed Order of Worship adopted by the Session, and shall ordinarily run for approximately ninety (90) minutes.
2. The Session will publish and maintain the printed Order of Worship and provide copies for the congregation; deviations shall be rare and announced in advance.

Article II —A Time of Pastoral Prayer, Edification, and Ministry (replacement for “activation”)
1. Each service shall include a designated time for pastoral prayer, ministries of edification, testimony, and the praying of the elders for particular needs (commonly called a “ministry time”).
2. Such ministry time shall be exercised only by elders or persons authorized by the Session, shall be governed by Scripture, and shall be practiced in an orderly manner befitting corporate worship (1 Corinthians 14:26–40).
3. No element of the service, including this ministry time, shall be taught or held out as the only or exclusive channel by which saving or renewing grace is given; God’s ordinary means of grace—preaching of the Word, the sacraments, and prayer—remain primary and sufficient.

Article III — Pastoral Touch and Physical Boundaries
1. Pastoral laying on of hands for prayer may be offered with the informed consent of the recipient. No member shall be required to submit to laying on of hands.
2. No member shall be required to perform any particular physical action (for example, falling backward) to “receive” a prayer or blessing. How a person receives pastoral prayer is a matter of conscience and pastoral discretion.
3. No one who declines a particular pastoral touch or physical posture shall be recorded, labeled, or treated as “resisting the flow.” Pastors and elders shall respond to refusals with gentleness, instruction, and, if appropriate, private pastoral conversation.

Article IV — Singing
1. Sung praise in our worship shall be drawn from the congregation’s approved psalter-and-hymn list, as overseen and periodically revised by the Session.
2. Additions to the approved list shall be made only after Session review for doctrinal soundness and fitness for worship.

Article V — Monthly Care and Accountability Meeting (careful, biblical practice)
1. The congregation shall hold a monthly members’ meeting devoted to mutual exhortation, pastoral care reporting, and corporate accountability.
2. Members are encouraged to practice private repentance, to confess sins to God, and to seek pastoral counsel and, where Scripture requires, public confession for scandalous and public sins (as the Session, in line with the Standards, shall define).
3. Members shall not be required to make public confession of private affections (such as momentary jealousy) before the whole membership. Where envy or jealousy has led to sinful public offense or scandal, the Session may require appropriate confession and restoration steps in accordance with Scripture and the processes of church discipline.

Article VI — Discipline, Conscience, and Enforcement
1. Members who covenant to this document submit to its terms and to the Session’s oversight insofar as those terms accord with Holy Scripture and the Standards to which this church subscribes.
2. The Session is entrusted to enforce this Covenant with pastoral care, Scripture-based correction, and the means of admonition, suspension, or exclusion only when Scripture so requires. Discipline shall always respect the liberty of conscience, the dignity of persons, and the processes described in the Scriptures and the Westminster Standards.
3. Any member who believes an enacted practice contradicts Scripture or conscience may bring the matter to the Session. If after careful consideration the Session persists in a practice that an individual believes to be contrary to Scripture, the member retains the right of private appeal and, as a last resort of conscience, withdrawal of membership in keeping with the liberty taught in our Standards.

Article VII — Amendments
1. This Covenant may be amended by a two-thirds vote of the active members present at a duly called members’ meeting, after receiving the recommendation of the Session and public notice of the change at least four weeks prior.
2. Amendments must be consistent with Holy Scripture and the Westminster Standards to which this congregation is pledged.

Short answer: B is worse than A. The decisive consideration is sustained, systematic oppression of many vulnerable people by someone entrusted with authority; cumulative, repeated injuries and loss of livelihood are a greater aggravation than a single malicious outburst, however vile.

Reasoning from the Westminster standards (summarized application)
- The Westminster Standards teach that sins differ in degree and are aggravated by factors such as malice and delight in another’s hurt, premeditation and deliberate repetition, relation to the offended (especially when one has trust or authority), and the number and weakness of victims. They also make clear that those in public trust must rule justly and protect the weak; to violate that trust and to oppress the vulnerable is a grave offense.

What aggravates each case, and the single thing that defines each
- Option A (single, gleeful public humiliation of a grieving worker)
  - Aggravations: malicious intent and delight in another’s suffering; public humiliation; attacking someone in acute grief; breach of pastoral/collegial duty to show mercy; abuse of supervisory power in the moment.
  - Defining feature (one thing that most defines A): malicious relish — deliberate enjoyment of another’s pain.

- Option B (quiet, methodical, year‑long belittling of many vulnerable workers)
  - Aggravations: sustained, repeated behavior (premeditation and pattern); multiple victims across shifts; targeting the weakest and those with disabilities; cumulative harm including lowered morale and resignations (loss of livelihood/opportunity); betrayal of trust inherent in supervisory office; systemic corrosive effect on the workplace.
  - Defining feature (one thing that most defines B): systematic, prolonged oppression of the weak by someone entrusted to manage and protect them.

Why B is worse than A (decisive consideration)
- The Standards count repetition, premeditation, the number and weakness of victims, and breach of public trust as serious aggravations. A single malicious assault of temper (A) is highly sinful and especially vile because of the relish; but B represents a deliberate, prolonged misuse of authority that grinds down many vulnerable people and produces lasting consequences (quitting, sustained discouragement). The multiplication of victims and the sustained betrayal of the supervisory office make B the more heinous wrong.

Ranking (least to most heinous), with the decisive consideration stated at each step
- Least: A — decisive consideration: single incident, albeit malicious, limited in duration and fewer victims.
- Most: B — decisive consideration: sustained, systematic oppression of many vulnerable people by an officer of trust.

3) Films and Shows (Content Standards)
- We do not watch films, shows, or other visual media that glorify cruelty or violence, mock the Christian faith, or are sexually explicit. Content will be judged by its actual substance and effect on the viewer, not only by rating or marketing.
- Parents will make case-by-case determinations. If you disagree about a judgment, bring your concerns respectfully; we will discuss it and the parents will explain the ruling.

5) How We Obtain Media (Lawful Use)
- We will only use legally obtained accounts and subscriptions consistent with the provider’s terms of service. We will not knowingly engage in piracy or theft of digital goods.
- If a family member offers us access to a shared account, we will confirm that its shared use is permitted under that provider’s terms before using it. We will not rely on or encourage dishonest behavior to obtain media.
- If the cost of a desired service is a concern, talk to the parents; we will decide on lawful, transparent solutions as a family (e.g., sharing a family plan within terms, choosing affordable services, or agreeing to purchase specific content).

- Parents will pre-watch or consult trustworthy reviews before younger children view any show, film, or media. If pre-watching is not possible, parents will consult reputable, faith-informed review sources.

Short answer first: I will not simply back you on both. The Westminster standards teach both that covetousness is a sin to be repented of and that lawful industry and provision for one’s family are duties. Which of those applies depends on motive, means, and the neglect of other duties. Read that way, the standards do not authorize you to dismiss your wife’s wishes as “discontent” without careful pastoral care, nor do they license you to run yourself and your family into spiritual and relational ruin in the name of “stewardship.” Here is how I would counsel you from the Westminster teaching.

1) What the standards require and forbid (briefly)
- Covetousness. The catechisms and confession treat covetousness as an inordinate desire for another’s goods or for things above our station; Christians are required to be content with God’s provision and to mortify sinful desires (the sense of the Tenth Commandment in the Standards).
- Industry and providence. The Standards also honour provident diligence and lawful labour: believers are to use God’s means, work to provide for their families, and be good stewards of time and talents.
- Duties to family and worship. Husbands are required to provide for, rule, and nourish their families in the Lord and to take care that children receive godly instruction. The Sabbath and public worship are to be observed; wanton neglect of the Lord’s Day and of family duties is condemned.

2) Applying that to your wife’s part‑time job
- Motive matters. A modest part‑time bookkeeping job, taken “to have a little of her own” and to get out a few mornings, is not automatically covetous. If her motive is legitimate (fellowship, usefulness, skill use, a bit of independent spending, contributing to family needs, mental health) then the job can be a lawful and even laudable calling.
- Covetousness is inward. The Standards locate the sin of covetousness primarily in the heart. You should not brand her motives as covetous without careful, loving inquiry and prayerful examination of both her heart and yours.
- Household roles and mutual submission. The Westminster teaching on marriage affirms distinct duties, mutual love and submission, and the prudent ordering of household affairs. Those teachings call for discussion and mutual agreement about how family resources and labours are arranged, not for unilateral prohibition by the husband.
- Practical counsel about the job: ask why she wants it, how it affects the household, whether it helps or hinders family worship and duties, and whether the money is used rightly. If her work genuinely sows division or is pursued for vain status, call that sin and repent. If it serves the family and her calling, honor it rather than accuse.

3) Applying that to your long hours and motive to “out‑earn” someone
- Motive again is decisive. The Standards condemn envy and covetous ambition. Setting a target to out‑earn your brother‑in‑law because he brags is a dangerous motive: it looks like envy, pride, and the love of the world — things the Standards and Scripture call us to mortify.
- Stewardship has limits. Provident diligence does not mean exhausting yourself or abandoning marital, parental, and religious duties. The duty to provide must be balanced with other duties: leading your family in the Lord, teaching children, preserving health, and keeping the Lord’s Day. Neglecting public worship because “Sundays sell best” is not acceptable in the Westminster understanding except for true necessity — and even then, one must seek ways to keep holy the Sabbath.
- Sabbath and family worship. The confession insists Christians keep the Lord’s Day for public and private worship. Repeatedly skipping church to sell is an obvious breach of that duty unless there is urgent, unavoidable necessity and provision has been made for worship at another time.
- Practical counsel about your work: examine your heart and repent of envy/competition; re‑set motives toward loving provision and stewardship rather than rivalry; scale back to a sustainable schedule that preserves family time, rest and the Lord’s Day; restore regular church attendance; keep one full day of rest if at all possible.

4) How to proceed together (practical steps from the Standards’ spirit)
- Mutual, humble conversation. Sit down together in a calm spirit, confess any sinful motives, and seek mutual understanding. The Standards require mutual love, not unilateral command.
- Examine motives in prayer and with pastoral help. Get a pastor or elder to help you both examine motives (covetousness vs. godly industry). The Standards value church discipline and pastoral oversight in difficult cases.
- Set boundaries and a plan. Agree on work hours, family priorities, Sabbath observance, and what the part‑time job’s money will be used for. Make a plan to restore weekly worship and parental duties.
- Repent where needed. If your aim has been to compete with your brother‑in‑law, confess and turn from that. If she has been hoarding or pursuing status, address that. Repentance and renewed affections for Christ and family are central.
- Steward money and time for kingdom ends. Reorient work toward provision, generosity, and service, not status. Use extra income for the church, needy, and necessary family expenses rather than for self‑glory.

Conclusion
The Westminster Standards do not give you license to bully your wife into quitting a modest job, nor do they bless your present course of unending hustling for the sake of beating a rival. They call you both to repent of covetousness, but they also call husbands to provide, families to be ruled in love, and Christians to observe the Lord’s Day. Love your wife; examine your own heart; restore worship and family life; and seek pastoral counsel so that your labours are truly godly stewardship rather than sinful striving. If you want, I can help you draft questions to ask your wife and a short plan you can present to a pastor or elders.

Short answer up front, by the norms of the Westminster Standards (Confession, Catechisms, and the Assembly’s Directory for Public Worship):

- (i) Stage lighting, fog, in‑ear click tracks — permitted as “circumstances” (things indifferent) provided they are used to serve true worship, kept decent and orderly, and not made into a means of superstition or spectacle. In other words: free, with prudent limits.

- (ii) Intentionally structuring a set to manufacture a wave of feeling — mixed. Musical shaping (dynamics, repetition, key changes, pauses) is also a circumstance and may be used to help the congregation attend to God; intentionally manipulating people to produce an emotional high that is then presented as a sure sign that “the Spirit is here” is forbidden. The leader may use musical craft to aid worship, but must not claim physical sensations (goosebumps, tears, etc.) as proof of the Spirit’s presence or let manufactured emotion displace Word‑centred, God‑ordained means of grace.

- (iii) Improvised “impressions” delivered as messages from the Lord to particular people — not permitted in public worship. The Westminster Standards condemn enthusiasm and private revelations presented as authoritative; public worship must be ordered according to Scripture and the church’s rule, and not by personal, immediate revelations.

Why, in the Standards’ terms
- The Confession and the Directory teach the regulative principle: the acceptable way of worship is instituted by God and therefore limited by His revealed will. Elements of worship are those God has appointed; other things are lawful only insofar as they are proper circumstances and do not invent worship or introduce superstition (i.e. “will‑worship” or “enthusiasm”).  
- The Assembly’s Directory warns against rhapsodical or vagabond speeches, unscriptural exhibition of private revelations, and devices that turn worship into a show rather than God‑ordained worship.

Practical counsel to present to the elders
1. Separate theology from style. Agree on principle first: adopt a short written worship polity rooted in the WCF/Directory language — regulative principle; worship elements are ordained by Scripture; circumstances may be used but must be subordinate to the Word and sacraments.  
2. Make clear rules:
   - Technical aids (lighting, fog, in‑ear click) may be used but with limits (safety, visibility, not obscuring preaching/sacrament, not distracting). Set measurable boundaries (fog density, lighting cues, no strobe that disorients, volume limits).  
   - Musical arrangement and dynamics are permissible to promote reverence and attention; leaders must not present manufactured feelings as the Spirit’s proof. Pastoral language: if the leader wants to invite response, it must be framed as an invitation to repent/come to Christ or to engage in a worship response grounded in the preached Word — not as “the Spirit is here” because people have goosebumps.  
   - No claiming of private revelations as direct messages from God in public worship. “Impressions” may be given as personal pastoral observations only, clearly labeled as such, and always submitted to eldership oversight; anything presented as a word from the Lord for the congregation must be evaluated, biblical, and — as a practical rule — avoided in public unless it is plainly Scripture‑based and the elders have judged it.

3. Provide accountability. Require that anyone who wants to give spontaneous words in a service discuss them with elders beforehand and submit them to Scripture and congregational edification tests (1 Cor. 14 principles: intelligibility, edification, order — which the Assembly’s Directory reflects in spirit). If this is part of the worship leader’s habitual practice, require training and correction; repeated disobedience merits pastoral discipline.

4. Reorder priorities in worship practice. Make preaching, the sacraments, and Scripture the centre. Any musical or technical means should point to those, not substitute for them.

If you want, I can draft a short worship policy (one page) you could present to the session that puts these Westminster principles into clear, actionable rules for your team.

Short answer (ruling from the Standards)
- Feature A (Scripture‑reading planner with reminders and optional streaks; sermon audio library): Lawful. Elders ought not to forbid this as a lawful aid. The app may be provided, but prudently designed and pastorally explained so it is not abused or presented as a substitute for true means of grace.
- Feature B (AI that each morning composes a first‑person “word from the Lord” tailored to the user): Unlawful to present as “the Lord’s” direct word. The Westminster Standards require that God’s revelation be received in Scripture and forbid giving or receiving pretended private revelations or adding new modes of divine speech. If a devotional feature is desired, it must be clearly presented as human (or machine‑assisted) devotional material — never as God speaking.

Reasoning from the Standards

1) On “things indifferent” and forbidding lawful helps
- The Confession teaches Christian liberty and that God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF XX.2). Christians are not bound by human inventions in matters indifferent, and the church should not require or forbid things contrary to Scripture. The Shorter Catechism answers that the Word of God (the Scriptures) is the only rule to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy God (Shorter Catechism Q.2). Private, lawful means of grace and aids which are not commanded or forbidden in Scripture (adiaphora) may be used so long as they do not contravene God’s revealed will or injure others’ consciences.
- A reading planner, reminders, and an audio sermon library are tools to help Christians read Scripture and hear preaching — lawful means of grace. To forbid such a tool simply because it uses modern technology (reminders, streaks) would be to impose a human prohibition on a lawful aid. That is impermissible under the Confession’s teaching about liberty of conscience and matters indifferent.

Pastoral application for Feature A
- Ship the feature, but design it pastorally:
  - Make reminders and “streaks/points” optional and user‑toggleable (not forced).
  - Avoid language or UI that implies that streaks equal spiritual status or God’s favor.
  - Provide in‑app teaching (short note or FAQ) about the goal: steady growth in grace, not performance or earning God’s favor.
  - Keep sermon audio clearly marked (sermon title, preacher, date, Scripture text) so users understand these are preaching/teaching, not new revelation.
  - Provide options for disabling gamification for those who find it spiritually harmful.
- If an elder’s conscience objects, they may refrain from using the feature, but they should not bind the church to the prohibition (WCF XX.2–3 on conscience and not wounding others).

2) On claiming God is speaking outside Scripture
- The Standards are adamant that Scripture is the rule of faith and life (Shorter Catechism Q.2; WCF I). The church must not invent worship or add other modes of divine revelation (WCF XXI.1: “The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men’s minds.”).
- Presenting AI‑generated, personalized first‑person messages as “a word from the Lord” is inherently dangerous and theologically impermissible. It would attribute divine speech to messages that are not Scripture and that have no apostolic authority; it risks encouraging trust in private or fabricated revelations and substitutes for the ordinary means of grace. That falls afoul of the Confession’s warnings against will‑worship, novelties, and false pretended revelations.

Pastoral application for Feature B
- Do not ship the feature as proposed. Specifically:
  - Never label AI output as “God said,” “the Lord told you,” or “your word from the Lord.”
  - Do not allow content that purports to be prophetic/direct revelation to individuals.
- If you want a morning devotional feature, reframe it along these lines:
  - “Daily Devotional,” “Daily Meditation,” or “Pastoral Reflection” — written by ministers or edited by pastors, or clearly labeled as AI‑generated devotional prompts and supervised/edited by human pastors.
  - Make explicit disclaimers: these are human (or machine‑assisted) reflections intended to encourage Scripture reading, prayer, and pastoral care, not fresh revelation or replacement of Scripture.
  - If AI is used to draft devotional content, require human editorial review by ordained ministers, and include a clear label “Edited/Reviewed by [pastor’s name]” and “Not a word from the Lord.”
- Encourage users with pastoral prompts to test the content by Scripture and bring concerns to their elders — align content with Scripture and orthodox teaching.

Conscience, unity, and governance
- The elder who would forbid Feature A is overstepping if he attempts to bind the church to his private judgment on an adiaphoron; the church should not forbid lawful helps (WCF XX.2–3).
- The elder who would authorize Feature B as though it were God’s speech is promoting an unlawful innovation in how God’s revelation is given; elders must guard the flock from such novelties (WCF XXI; WCF XXIII–XXV on teaching and discipline).
- If elders remain deadlocked, put the concrete proposals before the session with clear motions that embody the pastoral safeguards above (A: approve with optional gamification and explanatory wording; B: disapprove in its present form; approve an alternative devotional feature that is clearly labeled human/edited). If necessary, seek advice from the presbytery or higher court in keeping with your polity.

Brief example wording to use in the app and in elder communications
- For Feature A (in‑app): “This reading plan and sermon library are tools to help you engage Scripture and hear our preaching. Reminders and streaks are optional encouragements, not measures of godliness.”
- For any daily devotional alternative to Feature B: “Daily Devotion: A pastoral reflection (written/edited by our ministry team). Not a new revelation; read in light of Scripture.”

Conclusion
- Feature A: lawful, should not be forbidden; implement with pastoral restraint and options for those who are harmed by gamification.
- Feature B: unlawful as presented; do not present AI messages as God’s direct word. Provide only devotional material that is plainly human (or carefully edited by pastors and honestly labeled), and always subordinate to Scripture.

Short answer up front
- Wanting a better job and better pay is not automatically the sin of covetousness. The Tenth Commandment forbids inordinate, unlawful desire for another’s goods; it does not make every lawful desire for improvement sinful. It is possible to desire better pay for godly reasons (to provide for family, to serve more fruitfully) rather than out of a ruling love of money.
- Secretly copying a client list and a proprietary pricing playbook and taking them to a new employer is wrong. That is a breach of trust and amounts to stealing or misappropriation; the fact your manager has sinned does not justify your doing so. The Standards call Christians to honesty in their callings and to make restitution for wrongs.

How the Westminster Standards apply (plainly)
- The Westminster standards treat the moral law (summarized in the Ten Commandments) as binding on the heart as well as the life. They therefore properly identify covetousness as an inward sin — an inordinate desire for what belongs to another — but they do not forbid lawful, moderate desires for improvement or provision. “Contentment” is commended, but the Standards also teach that we are to perform our duties faithfully in our callings and to seek the good of our household and neighbor. In short: desires must be judged by whether they are lawful, ordered to God, and not an idol ruling the heart.
- The Standards also insist on honesty, faithfulness, and doing good works in one’s calling. Secretly taking an employer’s files, client lists, or trade secrets is a breach of honesty and fidelity to one’s neighbor; that is forbidden. Where injury has been done (by you or by others), sincere repentance and, where possible, restitution is required.

Questions for conscience and counsel
Before you act, examine motives and facts:
- Why do you want the new job? Is it primarily to serve God better and care for those God has entrusted to you, or mainly to gratify status/money? Desire for provision and a healthier workplace is often legitimate; a ruling love of money is not.
- Would taking the interview be dishonest? No — interviewing is a normal, lawful thing. You can seek employment in godly freedom.
- What exactly is proprietary or confidential at your current employer? Are there explicit company policies, signed agreements (non‑solicit, confidentiality, IP), or legal constraints? Many client lists and pricing strategies are company property even if you compiled them.
- Do you already have the files copied? If you have taken them, you should not keep or use them. The Standards require repentance and making restitution where possible.

Practical, faithful steps (what I would counsel you to do)
1. Pray and examine your heart. Ask God to reveal whether your desire is lawful and rightly ordered rather than covetousness. Seek the counsel of a faithful elder or pastor who knows you.
2. Take the interview. Looking for a better job is not sin in itself. You may accept where God opens doors and where you can serve faithfully.
3. Do not take or use proprietary company materials without clear permission. Do not secretly copy client lists, playbooks, pricing files, or other trade secrets. That is a breach of the duty of honesty and would be wrongful even if your manager has been guilty of sin.
4. If clients are genuinely your personal contacts (you know them personally and they would choose to follow you), it is not inherently dishonest to maintain relationships. But proceed carefully: don’t use copied confidential data, and respect any contractual restrictions.
5. If you are bound by contract (confidentiality, non‑solicit, non‑compete), get clarity — read the contract and, if needed, seek legal advice. Acting wisely protects you and your witness.
6. If you have already copied files, remove them promptly, confess to appropriate authorities (and to God), and make restitution where possible. The Standards teach repentance and restitution for wrongs.
7. Address the workplace abuse by proper means if possible: keep records, speak to HR or an appropriate official, and seek redress. But do not return evil for evil; pursue justice lawfully and Christianly.

A pastoral note
You are not required to suffer ongoing belittling, underpayment, or a toxic environment in silence. The Christian life includes lawful stewardship of one’s abilities and care for one’s family. Seeking a better position can be a faithful exercise of that stewardship. At the same time, the way you leave and the way you secure a new position must reflect the holiness, honesty, and love called for by the moral law — even toward those who have wronged you.

- suggest questions to help you examine your heart in light of Scripture and the Standards, or
- draft a brief, honest exit plan that protects your witness and legal standing.

Short answer up front
- From the standpoint of the Westminster Standards, what you did was a serious wrong (deception and taking money under false pretenses) and genuine repentance will require more than inward sorrow: it requires confession where appropriate, forsaking the sin, and making restitution to those you have injured. Quietly giving the money to charity is not an adequate substitute for repaying those you directly deceived unless they consent to that arrangement.
- Practically: admit the wrongdoing to the people wronged, offer to make them whole (refunds, or their explicit agreement to a different remedy), set up a transparent restitution plan if you cannot pay all at once, consult your church elders/pastor for spiritual oversight, and keep careful records. Below I give a draft disclosure and a simple, fair refund structure you can adapt.

The moral ground (briefly, in Westminster terms)
- The Westminster Standards teach that true repentance is not only remorse but turning from sin and doing works meet for repentance, including making right what you have wronged. Deceiving people and taking money for something you knew to be fraudulent is a sin against both God and your neighbor; where a sin has hurt another, restitution is required to the extent you can make it.
- Charity to the poor is good, but it does not discharge your duty to those you directly injured. You may, after you have made restitution or with the consent of the injured parties, give to charity as an expression of repentance; you should not use charity to avoid confessing and restoring those you wronged.

Practical steps to take now
1) Immediate pastoral action
- Confess this to your pastor/elders and ask for their counsel and accountability. The Standards expect oversight in repentance and will help you avoid self‑justifying cover‑ups and will guide you in making amends.

2) Stop the practice (you already have) and document what happened
- Preserve records: dates of sessions, names and contact info, payments taken, and any intake material that was used. This is necessary for accurate restitution.

3) Set aside a restitution fund
- Immediately segregate the money you estimate is owed (your $30k figure or as you can verify) into a separate account so it cannot be spent on other things.

4) Notify the people wronged (honest confession)
- Write a plain, humble disclosure to the 140 clients, admitting the deception, taking responsibility, offering restitution, and giving instructions for how they can request a refund or choose another remedy. Be short, clear, unambiguous, and avoid minimizing or excusing what happened.

5) Offer restitution, with a transparent schedule if you cannot pay at once
- Offer full refunds to anyone who asks. If you cannot pay all claims immediately, propose a standardized repayment plan (see suggested options below), prioritized by request date or by greatest demonstrated need. Keep clients informed and issue receipts when payments are made.

6) Be willing to accept consequences
- Reputation loss, bad reviews, financial strain—these are burdens you must accept as part of making things right.

7) After restitution is complete
- Only after you have made direct restitution should you consider charitable gifts as an outward sign of repentance and to make additional good. If any client explicitly wants you to donate on their behalf rather than receive a refund, document that consent.

Draft disclosure you can send
Subject: A personal apology, a confession, and an offer to make things right

Dear [Name],

I am writing to you with a heavy but necessary confession and to offer a way to make things right.

From [dates], I offered and charged for “ancestral clearing” sessions at [studio name]. I told clients I was channeling guidance from departed relatives. That was not true. I improvised and used intake material to create the sessions. I now see that this was deceptive and sinful. I am deeply sorry for misleading you and for taking money under false pretenses.

I have stopped offering those sessions and am repenting of this practice. I want to make restitution. If you received one or more ancestral clearing sessions from me and would like a refund, I will provide it. Please reply to this email by [date — e.g., 30 days from sending] and indicate:
- the date(s) of the session(s) and amount you paid, and
- whether you would like (A) a full refund returned to the original payment method, (B) a refund by a scheduled payment plan, or (C) to decline a refund.

If you do not respond by [date], I will follow up once more; after that I will hold the funds for as long as is reasonable and seek counsel from my church elders about next steps.

If you prefer to speak by phone, call [phone number] or request a time and I will call you. I will process refunds as quickly as I can and will send a receipt for every payment.

If you would prefer that I donate on your behalf to a bereavement or grief support charity instead of receiving a refund, please say so explicitly; I will honor that instruction.

I deeply regret this sin and the harm it caused. I ask your forgiveness, and I am committed to making this right before God and before you.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Studio name, contact info]

How to structure refunds if you cannot pay all at once
- Step 1 — Tally and set aside: Verify exact amounts paid and set that total aside in a restitution account.
- Step 2 — Offer a simple, standard schedule so everyone is treated fairly rather than negotiating ad hoc. Example options you can give clients:
   Option 1 — Immediate full refund (if you can pay). First priority will be given to those who request immediate refund and to those who demonstrate financial hardship.
   Option 2 — Fixed installment plan: equal payments over 6 or 12 months (for example, total refund ÷ 12, with first payment within 30 days). You make monthly payments until paid in full.
   Option 3 — Deferred short-term lump-sum: smaller payment now with a committed date for balance (e.g., $X now, balance by [date within 6 months]).
   Option 4 — Refund by credit to current legitimate services only if the client explicitly chooses that instead of cash.
   Option 5 — If the client explicitly agrees, you may give an equivalent charitable donation on their behalf instead of refunding them.
- Step 3 — Commit to a timetable publicly (in the disclosure or in a follow-up message) and produce monthly statements of payments made and remaining balances if installment plans are used.
- Step 4 — Keep absolute documentation: client requests, agreements, payment amounts & dates, receipts.
- Step 5 — Prioritize hardship and the order of requests. Be transparent about capacity: e.g., “I can presently pay $X per month toward refunds; I will distribute that amount pro rata among those requesting refunds unless a person documents urgent hardship.”

Practical wording for a reply form (short)
Please reply with:
1) Date(s) of session(s) and amount paid.
2) Which option you choose: A (full refund), B (installment refund), C (deferred lump-sum), D (credit for current services), or E (donation on my behalf).
3) If choosing B or C, include preferred bank or payment details and best contact number.

Some pastoral and legal cautions
- Involve your pastor/elders: they can help mediate, hold you accountable, and walk with you through the process of restitution and reconciliation.
- Consider legal counsel if you have concerns about liability or if any client threatens legal action. But remember legal liability does not remove the moral duty to confess and make restitution.
- Be prepared that some people will be angry or refuse restitution offers; you still have the duty to make a full, documented effort to repair the wrong.

A few final words
- Doing the honest, costly thing now will harm your reputation in the short term but honors Christ, shows true repentance, and will ultimately be the most faithful witness. The Standards call Christians to confession and to making right harms done to neighbors. Quietly diverting money to charity to salve your conscience is not sufficient.
- I know this is hard. Take these steps with pastoral oversight, and follow through faithfully until every reasonable claim has been satisfied or until your church leadership advises otherwise.

Preamble / Covenant
We, [Partner A name] and [Partner B name], brothers (sisters) in Christ, covenant together before God and one another to run our business in a manner faithful to Holy Scripture and to the moral teaching we submit to as Christians (including our understanding of the moral law as set forth in the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms). In particular we acknowledge that covetousness, deceit, and breach of our vows are sins we must avoid; we therefore bind ourselves in love and conscience to the following Integrity & Contentment Agreement (the “Agreement”), to govern our conduct so that our enterprise may serve God, bless our neighbors, and be a witness to the gospel.

1. Definitions and Term
1.1 “Partnership” means the business carried on under the name [Business Name].
1.2 “Partner” means either signatory to this Agreement.
1.3 “Partnership Term” means the period from the Effective Date below until dissolved by mutual written agreement of both Partners or by operation of law.
1.4 “Key Employee or Client” means an employee or client who materially contributes (as determined by mutual agreement and documented in writing) to at least [specify threshold, e.g., 10%] of Partnership revenue or operations.
1.5 This Agreement is effective as of the Effective Date below and will remain in force through the Partnership Term unless amended as provided in Section 11.

2. Covenant against Outside Competing Ambition (Term, Non‑Compete)
2.1 During the Partnership Term neither Partner shall, directly or indirectly, (a) start or operate a business that competes with the Partnership’s principal lines of business, (b) solicit or accept a materially better outside employment offer or partnership in a competing business, or (c) take on any business activity that diverts time, attention, or materially reduces the Partner’s ability to perform duties for the Partnership, except with the prior written consent of the other Partner.
2.2 We make this covenant because Scripture and our confession warn against covetousness and the divided heart. A breach of this clause is a breach of this Agreement and, because it undermines the trust on which the Partnership stands, will entitle the non‑breaching Partner to the remedies set out in Section 10.

3. Resentment, Confession, and Monthly Meeting
3.1 We agree to meet at least once each month (the “Monthly Meeting”) for business review and mutual spiritual and pastoral accountability. At each Monthly Meeting we will review financials, important decisions, and relational matters.
3.2 If either Partner feels resentment, envy, or an injurious spirit because the other Party received a larger draw, greater recognition, or other favorable outcome in any given period, that feeling shall be confessed promptly at the next Monthly Meeting. The confessing Partner will state the cause of the feeling so the Partners may pray, counsel, and pursue reconciliation in the spirit of Matthew 18 and the Westminster teaching on duties to one another.
3.3 Minutes of the Monthly Meeting shall be kept and access to those minutes will be open to both Partners.

4. Hiring or Acquisition of Competitor’s People or Clients; Sharing Gain
4.1 If during the Partnership Term either Partner (the “Hiring Partner”) hires away a Key Employee or secures a Key Client from a direct competitor by offering materially better terms, the incremental economic benefit (the “Gain”) attributable to that new employee or client in the 12 months following that hire or first work for the client shall be accounted for and split equally between the Partners, after deducting reasonable acquisition costs directly attributable to securing that hire or client.
4.2 “Gain” shall be calculated by comparing Partnership net profit for the relevant 12‑month period with and without the revenue/expense attributable to that Key Employee or Client, using the Partnership’s regular accounting methods. If Partners cannot agree on calculation, they will appoint a mutually acceptable independent CPA to determine the Gain, whose determination will be binding.
4.3 This clause does not authorize any unlawful or deceitful methods of recruitment or solicitation. The Partners affirm that all recruitment and client acquisition will be done honestly and lawfully.

5. Honest Books; Full Access
5.1 Each Partner shall cause the Partnership to keep full, accurate, and current books and records in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles consistently applied, and shall not conceal any material matter from the other Partner.
5.2 Each Partner shall have full access, at reasonable times, to inspect and copy the Partnership’s books, records, bank accounts, contracts, and other pertinent documents. Monthly financial statements shall be prepared and provided in advance of each Monthly Meeting.

6. Truthful Competition; No False Undercutting
6.1 Neither Partner shall undercut, defame, or disparage a competitor by knowingly making false statements or misleading claims about a competitor’s product, service, or reputation.
6.2 All marketing and competitive claims must be truthful, verifiable, and consistent with our duty to love our neighbor and to refrain from lying or injuring another unfairly, as taught in the Westminster Standards.

7. Tithing and Priority of Gospel Support
7.1 Before drawing personal salary or distributions, the Partnership shall set aside ten percent (10%) of net profits each fiscal year (the “Tithe”), payable to gospel work, church, or missions approved by mutual agreement of the Partners.

Short answer: what you describe in T2 contains essential and necessary elements of repentance, but it is too broad and some parts (a public pulpit confession and permanent disqualification) are not automatically required and could do more harm than good unless handled under pastoral/elderly care and with Priya’s consent. The Westminster standards teach that true repentance produces confession, repair to those wronged, submission to the church’s discipline, and a changed life — so do the concrete things below, and let the elders guide public steps and any consequences.

Why (from the Westminster teaching)
- The Westminster Confession and Catechisms treat repentance as an evangelical grace: it must include sorrow for sin, confession, faith in Christ, and a serious reformation of life (fruits meet for repentance). Repentance is not merely inward grief but requires outward acts where the sin affected others.
- When sin has injured another’s person or reputation, the duty of repentance necessarily includes making satisfaction, confession, and reparation to the injured party and submitting to lawful church discipline intended to reclaim and restore (the church’s censures are remedial and aim at repentance and restoration).

Practical, concrete steps you should take (in order)

1) Immediate, humble repentance before God
- Confess this sin to the Lord, plead the blood and grace of Christ for forgiveness, and seek the Holy Spirit’s help to hate this sin and to change. This is the foundation.

2) Confess to your pastor/elders and accept their guidance
- Tell the pastor (and if the church has elders, bring it to them) the whole truth, ask their counsel, and subject yourself to whatever pastoral discipline they judge appropriate. The church’s officers exist to deal with sin in the congregation and to direct restoration. Be ready to accept consequences they judge fit.

3) Confess to Priya and seek personal reconciliation
- Meet with Priya (preferably with a neutral elder present if she wants that) and tell her plainly that you lied, explain why you did it (repentantly, not justifying), ask her forgiveness, and listen to how the lie harmed her. Ask what she thinks would be a fitting way to make things right. Making amends here is a biblical and WCF-consistent duty.

4) Make reparation where possible
- If her reputation needs restoring, offer to help repair it: correct the false impression with those who were told or affected (pastor, music team leaders, relevant members). But coordinate with Priya: you should not unilaterally make a public announcement that re-exposes her. Restoration of her standing should be done in a way that honors her and serves her healing.

5) Offer to step aside, at least for a season
- Offering to resign the worship-leader post and to make way for Priya (if she wants it) is a proper and humble act of reparation. It is especially appropriate while trust is being rebuilt. Whether you must permanently leave all church service is another matter: the Westminster standards require reformation of life and the church’s remedial discipline, not permanent exile if there is genuine repentance. Let the elders decide whether removal from office or a longer season away from public leadership is necessary.

6) Be careful about public pulpit confession
- The WCF and the practice of church discipline distinguish between private sins and sins that have been publicly scandalous. Only if the sin has been widely known and the scandal must be healed by public confession should a pulpit confession before the whole congregation be made — and even then it should be done under the elders’ direction and, importantly, in a way that seeks to restore the injured party rather than to stir gossip. Because the lie was known only to you and the pastor, a public pulpit confession is not automatically required and could do more harm (re-traumatize Priya, spread the lie afresh). Ask the elders and Priya whether/when and how any wider statement should be made.

7) Submit to church discipline and show lasting fruit
- If the elders impose censure, accept it willingly. The point of church discipline (per the Standards) is reclaiming and restoration. Demonstrate repentance by changed behavior over time, transparency, and humility.

8) Practical supports
- Keep a pattern of accountability, prayer, Bible reading, and possibly counseling. Reconciliation is a process; be patient and practical in rebuilding trust.

- Don’t make the situation about your public humiliation only. The aim of confession is to honor God, repair the wrong, and restore those injured. That may mean private confession and private reparation rather than dramatic public acts.
- Don’t decide for Priya what repairs she needs. Involve her and the elders. She may not want a public airing; she may want you to make a private apology and to help repair her reputation quietly.

Encouragement

The church’s work is to restore those who repent, not to cast them out permanently without cause.

Short answer: this was a misuse of members’ property and a breach of your fiduciary duty. The right way forward is to stop the practice immediately, disclose the matter to those with authority, make full restitution (or offer it and let the board decide the method of restoring members’ money), submit to any lawful or ecclesiastical discipline and civil process that may follow, and set and document a correct policy going forward. You should also seek legal counsel before making detailed public statements.

Grounding in the Westminster standards
- The Confession and Catechisms press that genuine repentance is more than inner sorrow: it issues in confession, forsaking the sin, making restitution where possible, and suffering the lawful consequences of our actions. The Larger and Shorter Catechisms teach that repentance includes acknowledgment of sin to God and the offended, a desire to make amends, and an honest effort to repair what was damaged. In short: moral guilt requires honest disclosure and repair, not concealment or rationalization.
- You have a duty of justice and truth toward those you wronged (the members) and to the office you held. The fact that the funds were not personally pocketed does not remove the obligation: you decided the disposition of members’ money without authority.

Practical steps I recommend (ordered, with reasons)
1. Stop the practice and preserve records
   - Immediately cease any further use of the suspense account or of any similar rounding practice.
   - Preserve all books, electronic records, emails, and notes relating to the dividend calculations, the suspense account, the grants you made, and annual audits. Do not alter or destroy anything.

2. Consult an attorney
   - Before you give a full public account, consult an attorney experienced in nonprofit/credit-union law and fiduciary matters. There may be civil or criminal ramifications (embezzlement, conversion, breach of fiduciary duty, etc.) depending on state law and facts (intent, materiality, auditors’ sign-offs). Legal counsel will advise on timing and content of disclosures and on limiting personal exposure while you act to make things right.

3. Calculate and document the precise amounts
   - Work with the credit union’s accountant/auditor (and your attorney) to compute the exact total taken from members and, if feasible, the per-member amounts and how those were determined. Put this in writing for the board and for counsel.

4. Disclose to the board (and auditors) promptly and honestly
   - Make a factual, unembellished disclosure to the board of directors and the credit union’s management/legal counsel. Offer the records and your full cooperation. Concealing the matter or leaving it for others to discover will worsen moral and legal consequences.

5. Offer and effect restitution
   - Offer to restore the full sum you controlled (the $14,300 plus any interest if counsel advises). The board—whose duty it is to protect members’ interests—can decide the practical method to restore the benefit to members (pro rata credits to accounts, a special dividend, notice giving members the option to claim their share, or other equitable distribution). Because the money was taken from members, it should be returned to them, not redirected to third-party causes you approve.
   - If the board decides a full individual distribution is impractical, let them document publicly how they have judged the fairest and most cost-effective remedy. But you should not unilaterally decide to leave the past uncorrected.

6. Be prepared to accept consequences
   - Repentance includes submitting to lawful sanctions. That may include resignation (or being asked to resign), repayment terms, civil restitution orders, or, in some cases, criminal charges. Cooperate with any review or investigation and accept discipline from the board or church if applicable.

7. Make amends publicly and pastorally
   - After consultation with counsel and the board, offer an honest apology to the board and—if the board requests it—a clear, plain statement to the membership explaining what happened and what corrective steps were taken. Avoid minimization or rationalization. Let the membership see the effort to make restitution and the steps taken to prevent recurrence.

8. Put good governance in place going forward
   - Propose a written rounding/dividend policy, approved by the board, so the practice is transparent. Have dual controls, periodic independent review, and clear delegation for discretionary grants. Ensure audits are meaningful and that the board gets adequate reporting.

Addressing the co‑treasurer’s suggestion
- Leaving the past uncorrected because “chasing 900 people” is impractical is not ethically adequate. The burden of restoring stolen or misapplied funds falls on the wrongdoer and the responsible governing body; practicality cannot justify retaining or reallocating other people’s property without consent. The board can choose an administrable remedy. Your role is to disclose, offer restitution, and cooperate in whatever reasonable method the board chooses.

A suggested short disclosure to the board (adapt as advised by your attorney)

I apologize and will provide all records and help with an accurate accounting.”

Final pastoral note from the Standards
- The Westminster standards hold out mercy in Christ for the penitent, but that mercy is not a license to ignore justice. True repentance seeks to repair wrongs done to our neighbors and accepts just consequences. Acting promptly, honestly, and constructively is the way to begin making this right.

What the Standards require (brief)

- The Confession’s teaching about the church (see the chapters on church discipline) presumes that public and scandalous sins are to be confessed and corrected publicly and that the sinner should submit to appropriate remedial measures.  
- The Catechisms and the Confession together make clear that repentance requires making restitution and reparation so far as it can be done: you must seek to repair what your sin broke and to do the good you wrongly prevented.

What repentance and restitution should look like in this situation
1) Immediate repentance to God

Why (short theological/moral basis from the Westminster Standards)
- The Standards require true repentance: humiliation before God, confession, turning from the sin, making amends where possible, and submission to the church’s discipline (the elders) for public scandals. The elders are the officers appointed to judge and apply church censures and remedial measures.
- Charity and justice require protecting the innocent and avoiding scandalous disclosure that would slander or unnecessarily harm those who were deceived. Exposing people who did not know they were complicit would be unloving and bring unnecessary damage.
- Therefore the right course: immediate private confession to elders, private pastoral care and confession to those directly hurt, and then a public confession directed and framed by the elders.

Practical plan — who, in what order, and what to say (drafts included)

1) Immediate: confession to the elder board (as soon as possible; do this before you say anything to staff or volunteers)
- Why first: elders have canonical responsibility to shepherd the flock and to direct discipline and public disclosure (WCF: church censures). You must put yourself under their authority.

- Do not make public accusations about other staff unless they were knowingly complicit and elders direct naming.
- In short: do not expose innocent people, private information, or anything that will cause reputational harm where the person did not consent.

4) Public confession to the congregation (only after elders have given direction and approved wording/timing)

- Draft for a Sunday announcement (example):

Many of the volunteers involved were unaware that they were part of a plan — they are not to blame. I will submit to the elders’ direction about next steps, and I will do whatever they require to make amends and to restore trust. I ask your forgiveness and your prayers for those who were hurt. - Offer to meet privately with any person who believes they were harmed and to make personal restitution where possible.

- Submit to counseling and public accountability (regular check‑ins with elders).

Final note on conscience and submission
The Westminster Standards require both confession and submission to ecclesiastical authority, and charity toward brethren. Your first and indispensable acts now are (1) honest confession to God and to the elders, (2) full cooperation with whatever discipline or remedy they require, and (3) private pastoral care for those you deceived — not a public exposé that will compound harm.

Short answer first: you should not treat both calls as right. The Westminster Standards do distinguish lawful, diligent striving in a lawful calling from the sin of covetousness; and they treat envy, grudging, and injuring your neighbor’s good as plainly sinful. In plain terms: Member A is not automatically guilty of the tenth commandment simply because he wants to grow his business; what matters is whether his heart is discontent, envious, or inordinate. Member B’s bitterness and the secret bad‑mouthing are much more clearly violations of the tenth commandment and must be repented of.

Basis from the Standards (and what I’ll do next): the Westminster Larger Catechism sets out both the duties required by the tenth commandment and the sins forbidden by it; those are the primary texts to consult to decide cases like these. If you would like, I will pull and quote the exact verbatim wording from the Larger Catechism and (if you want) the Shorter Catechism or Confession. For now I’ll summarize the relevant teaching and apply it pastorally.

Summary of the relevant teaching (plain language tied to the Standards)
- The catechism teaches that the tenth commandment forbids covetousness, envy, grudging at another’s good, and all inordinate desires and motions to that which is another’s. It also enjoins contentment with our own condition and a charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbor (i.e., approving and delighting in his good, doing him good, and communicating to his needs).
- From that twin emphasis the Standards make two things plain:
  1. A desire to provide for your family, to use your gifts in a lawful calling, to seek expansion or a larger contract by honest effort, and to steward resources faithfully is not ipso facto covetousness. Industry, prudence, and lawful ambition in a lawful calling are legitimate (the catechism explains what is forbidden by the commandment, not that all desire to improve one’s lot is sinful).
  2. By contrast, envy, secret rejoicing at another’s loss or maliciously undermining a neighbor, speaking ill of him to steal customers, or fomenting hurtful schemes out of resentment are precisely the kind of sins the tenth commandment forbids.

How to apply to your two members (practical counsel)
- Member A (restless to grow after taking a loan): don’t tell him that ambition itself is always covetousness and that he must stop striving and accept his lot. Instead:
  - Help him examine his heart: is his desire rooted in love of God and neighbor, stewardship, provision for family, and a desire to use his gifts? Or is it rooted in discontent with what God has given, constant comparison with others, grudging at his neighbor’s prosperity, or an inordinate desire to possess what is another’s?
  - If it is the latter (discontent, envy), call him to repent, seek contentment, and cultivate gratitude and charity. If it is the former (lawful diligence, honest desire to steward and serve), encourage faithful, ethical striving—while guarding against covetousness.
  - Practical steps: confession and repentance if envy is present; cultivate contentment (prayer, Scripture, grateful practices); set ethical business practices and accountability; seek counsel about the loan and prudent stewardship.
- Member B (bitter, bad‑mouthed competitor): treat this as a clear breach. The Standards’ description of the sins under the tenth commandment includes envying your neighbor’s good and actions that harm or usurp his good. Secretly speaking ill of a neighbor to steal customers, nursing resentment, and taking pleasure in his loss are precisely the sort of things called sinful.
  - Call him to repent of the bitterness and the slander, to make restitution where possible (e.g., retraction/correction with those he maligned), and to seek to approve and delight in his neighbor’s good rather than undermine it.
  - Practical steps: confession to those wronged, public correction if necessary, stop the defamatory talk, seek reconciliation, and cultivate a charitable spirit (pray for the competitor, practice blessing them).

Why your original pair of judgments was inconsistent
- Telling Member A that any strong desire to grow is covetousness collapses lawful industry into sin. That is not what the Standards teach. They forbid inordinate desire, envy, and discontent, not every lawful desire to improve one’s condition.
- Telling Member B that his bitterness and secret bad‑mouthing is merely “healthy competitive fire” misses the catechism’s explicit prohibitions against envying and injuring another’s good. His actions are, under the Standards, disclosable sins that call for confession and restitution.

Short answer up front (as I would actually tell the team leader): both of your rulings are problematic under the Westminster Standards.

- Ruling 1 (keep the 40‑minute guided “picture Jesus / receive a word from him / altar response” meditation) is not consistent with the Standards’ strict “worship only as God has appointed” principle. The Standards require that worship and devotional practices be those God has appointed in his Word and forbid worship “in any other way not appointed” (i.e. invented or subjective modes of worship). Directing people to imagine a vividly seated Jesus and to receive “affirmations from him” as a personal holy word risks fostering private revelation and a kind of devised worship the Standards warn against. You should not tell attendees to expect a direct word from Christ as though it were a divine revelation; instead reframe any experiential element so it is explicitly governed by Scripture (Scripture reading, prayer, sober reflection on biblical text, and an invitation to respond to God in prayer), and make clear that any “impressions” are to be tested by Scripture and the elders.

- Ruling 2 (ban acoustic‑guitar prelude and warm low lighting as “man‑made mood manufacturing”) goes too far. The Westminster Standards require that public worship be instituted by God’s revealed will (so you may not invent rites), and they also protect Christian liberty of conscience so that the church ought not to bind or forbid indifferent practices which Scripture does not command or forbid.

Practical counsel
- Do not introduce the labyrinth walk, the borrowed “centering” breath‑prayer as a liturgical rite, or a self‑styled annual “ashes‑and‑oil anointing” into your congregation’s public worship as if they were divinely‑instituted acts of worship or additional sacraments. These are either invented rites or borrowed forms from other religious traditions; under the Standards such things may not be imposed as worship‑acts of the church.
- If some of these practices are pastorally helpful (e.g., a labyrinth used once as a private devotional pathway, or a short pastoral blessing with oil in exceptional cases), treat them as pastoral, voluntary, private or educational usages — not as public worship elements — and make clear they are optional and not sacramental.
- Do not forbid kneeling at confession, a brief silence, or a fixed start time unless you can show they are sinful or contrary to Scripture. Those are matters of circumstance and conscience; banning them across the congregation is an improper exercise of authority in matters the Standards leave free.
- Work by the Session/elders to discern and frame any change: keep worship to the elements God has appointed, distinguish sacraments from pastoral practices, and preserve conscience and charity among members (especially older members attached to certain forms).

Relevant Westminster citations (with the wording you requested)

1) The regulative principle for worship — worship must be instituted by God’s revealed will
- WCF 21.1: “The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of devils.” 

How this applies: the Confession teaches that the church must not conduct public worship according to human inventions or devices. A labyrinth walk used as a liturgical rite, a breath‑centering prayer ritual borrowed from another tradition and presented as part of public worship, or an annually instituted anointing rite designed by the church would be introduced practices not “instituted by himself,” and so fall under what the Confession forbids as man‑devised worship.

2) Liberty of conscience — do not bind or forbid indifferent practices which Scripture does not command
- WCF 20.2: “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in any thing contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship.”

How this applies: the Standards forbid ruling people’s consciences by human commands where Scripture is silent. That means you should not abolish or forbid kneeling at confession, a brief moment of silence, or the practice of starting at a fixed time merely because they are “man‑made” if they are not contrary to Scripture. Such postures, silences, and scheduling practices are matters of circumstance and conscience; the Session should not remove them as though they were sinful.

(If you want the fuller chapter text to consult: WCF chapter 21 deals with religious worship and the Sabbath day; chapter 20 deals with Christian liberty and liberty of conscience.)

A bit more explanation tying those two texts together
- WCF 21.1 tells the church it must not invent or adopt as worship what God has not instituted. That argues against adding new liturgical rites (labyrinth as a worship act, a foreign contemplative prayer presented as a liturgical norm, an invented annual anointing).
- WCF 20.2 protects the believer’s conscience from being bound by human traditions in things Scripture does not command. That argues against abolishing or forbidding indifferent practices (kneeling, silence, start times) that are not sinful or contrary to Scripture.

So your proposal is inconsistent with the Standards: you cannot permissively invent new worship rites that are not instituted by God while simultaneously forbidding other indifferent practices that Scripture does not command. The right course under the Standards is to confine public worship to what God has instituted, and to allow freedom (with pastoral guidance) in indifferent matters rather than imposing broad prohibitions.

Short answer: neither of you is fully right. The Westminster Standards teach both duties: a man must lawfully preserve and order his property (and see debts paid), and he must also relieve the poor and not practise oppression. That means Christian landlords may lawfully enforce rights, but only as stewards bound by justice and charity — so eviction ought not to be the first, default, or vindictive step where relief or reasonable forbearance (or church aid) will do. Below I give the standards you asked for and then practical counsel consistent with them.

Relevant citations (Westminster Shorter Catechism)
- WSC Q40 — “What is required in the eighth commandment?”  
  “The eighth commandment requireth the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others; and the preservation and lawful and diligent wasting of the same; and the study of industry and frugality; and the payment of our debts, and of such things as we are obliged to; and the relieving the poor and such as are in want.”
- WSC Q41 — “What is forbidden in the eighth commandment?”  
  “The eighth commandment forbiddeth whatsoever doth, or may, unjustly hinder our own, or our neighbour’s, wealth, or outward estate; as the taking away, or withholding that which is our neighbour’s, or of his right; and the unjust diminution, wasting, or disposing of our own or our neighbour’s goods; and the neglecting or refusing the performance of our promises and contracts; and all cheats, frauds, extortions, and oppression.”
- WSC Q103–Q105 — (tenth commandment) — relevant parts:  
  Q103: “Which is the tenth commandment?” — “The tenth commandment is, Thou shalt not covet.”  
  Q104: “What is required in the tenth commandment?” — “The tenth commandment requireth full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour, and all inward motions thereunto.”  
  Q105: “What is forbidden in the tenth commandment?” — “The tenth commandment forbiddeth all discontentment with our own estate, envying at the good of our neighbour, and all inordinate motions and desires to anything that is his.”

How these texts settle the dispute
- Your point (lawful stewardship, protection of property, payment of debts) is grounded in WSC Q40: Christians are required to “lawfully procur[e] and further[] the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others” and to see “the payment of our debts.” A landlord has a legitimate duty to preserve property and to expect rents to be paid when due.
- Your colleague’s point (charity, not oppressing a brother) is grounded in the same catechism: WSC Q40 requires “the relieving the poor and such as are in want,” and WSC Q41 forbids “oppression” and other unjust treatment. The tenth commandment calls for contentment and a “charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour,” so a landlord must not take advantage of, oppress, or act without compassion toward a brother in need.

Practical counsel consistent with the Standards
1. Treat eviction as last resort. The Standards require relieving the poor and forbid oppression. Before eviction, the church/finance committee ought to inquire into the tenant’s real need, the expected duration of unemployment, and whether temporary aid, a short-term rent reduction, or a repayment plan is available.
2. Protect stewardship and justice. The owner’s duty to preserve his estate and have debts paid means he is not morally obliged to cancel the debt permanently. If the owner cannot afford indefinite free tenancy, a reasonable, documented forbearance or a fixed short-term rent deferral with a repayment plan is faithful to both stewardship and charity.
3. Use the church’s resources first. If the congregation has means, the church may (and the Standards commend that it should) relieve a needy member rather than require the landlord to carry the whole burden. That keeps charity public and deliberate rather than shifting all risk onto a single brother.
4. Avoid coercion or sham “forgiveness.” If the church or landlord forgives rent, document whether it is a gift or a loan and whether it is conditional (time-limited). That prevents later disputes and honors the duty to be “faithful in our engagements” (WSC Q40).
5. Apply equity and keep conscience clear. If eviction becomes unavoidable, do it only after reasonable warning and after exhausting the charitable options. If you must seek rent, do so without extortion or added penalties beyond what is just (WSC Q41 forbids “extortion” and “oppression”).

Concrete steps for your committee right now
- Meet with the tenant to establish facts (how long unemployed, job prospects, other income, family needs).
- Calculate what short-term relief the landlord can afford without endangering his stewardship (e.g., reduce rent by X% for Y months; defer Y months with simple repayment over Z months).
- If the committee can’t cover the shortfall, bring the case to the congregation’s benevolence budget before requiring the landlord to write it off.
- If you grant forbearance, put the arrangement in writing (terms, duration, review date).
- If the tenant refuses reasonable arrangements or cannot provide a plan for returning to solvency, then — after fair warning and opportunity to remedy — it is not unbiblical for the landlord to enforce the lease.

Bottom line: the Westminster Standards require both justice for property owners and mercy toward the needy. They do not license either hard-hearted strictness or blanket, indefinite forgiveness that would amount to neglect of stewardship or create injustice for the owner. Apply both sets of duties: relieve the poor where you can, but do so in an orderly, documented way that respects the owner’s legitimate rights and stewardship responsibilities (WSC Q40–41; Q103–105).
